Lee 2020 keeps the PD law and the actuator net but moves the network one level up: its output is a modulation of a hand-designed periodic motion, not the motion itself. The problem this solves is exploration on rough terrain. A freshly initialised policy outputs noise. If noise means random joint targets, the robot falls within a second, every episode terminates early, and the reward carries almost no information about which direction of change was better. If instead the robot is already stepping in place when training begins, noise means slightly different steps, episodes last long enough to compare, and the reward becomes informative. The supplement states the first half of this directly: with reasonably tuned base frequency, step height, and initial phases, "a quadruped can stably step in place" (S3). The paper states the second half when it explains the output frame: defining the output in the horizontal frame "results in less premature termination at the beginning of the policy training, when the base motion is unstable due to random actions" (p. 8). The design pattern is called Policies Modulating Trajectory Generators, PMTG (Iscen et al. 2018). A trajectory generator produces a nominal periodic motion from a phase. The policy outputs two things: parameters that change how the generator runs, and a residual that is added to the generator's output. The target sent downstream is generator output plus residual. The generator is a prior, not a constraint: if the policy learns a large residual, it can override the nominal motion entirely. What the prior buys is a sensible starting point and a coordinate system in which "lift the foot a little more" is a small number. lee2020-fig4-highlight-c.png Fig. 4 (p. 7), panel C highlighted. Motion generation at 50 Hz: the policy emits leg frequencies and foot position residuals; four foot trajectory generators turn phases into nominal foot positions; the sum is the target. Motion tracking at 400 Hz: inverse kinematics, joint PD control, robot dynamics. The observations return to the policy. The action is a 16-vector (p. 8): Component Dimension What it changes leg frequency offsets f_i , i = 1, \dots, 4 4 how fast each leg's phase advances; the base frequency f_0 is fixed foot position residuals \Delta r_{f_i, T} 4 \times 3 = 12 added to the generator's output in the horizontal frame H_i The data flow from action to torque, with the dimensions that Table S4 and the text give (numbers in parentheses are vector sizes): pmtg-data-flow.svg From the 16 policy outputs to torque. Top band, 50 Hz: the four frequency offsets advance the leg phases, the generators turn phases into nominal foot positions, and the twelve residuals are added. Bottom band, 400 Hz: the target is rotated from H_i into the base frame, inverse kinematics gives joint targets, and joint PD control tracks them. Two feedback paths return to the policy: the phases as \langle\cos\phi_i, \sin\phi_i\rangle and the proprioceptive observation o_t . p.8 · The phase variable, and why it is fed back as cosine and sine Each leg carries a phase \phi_i \in [0, 2\pi) . The first half, \phi_i \in [0, \pi) , is the contact phase; the second half, [\pi, 2\pi) , is the swing phase. The phase advances at a rate set by a common base frequency plus the policy's per-leg offset, \phi_i(t) = \big(\phi_{i,0} + (f_0 + f_i)\,t\big) \bmod 2\pi, \qquad f_0 = 1.25\ \mathrm{Hz}, as printed on p. 8. Read f_0 + f_i as the rate at which the phase advances; the printed formula omits the 2\pi that would convert hertz to radians per second, and the structure is what matters. The base frequency is the trot frequency of the lab's earlier model-based controller (ref. 26), which is where a sensible prior comes from in practice: from the controller you already have. You have built this object. The GaitScheduler in Convex MPC Biped (My Article) is a phase \varphi_s(t) = \mathrm{frac}\!\left(\tfrac{t - t_0}{T_c} + \phi_s\right) per side, with a half-cycle offset between legs. Two differences here. The phase rate is a policy output, so the network can speed one leg up or slow it down, which lets it retime individual legs without a gait library. And the phase does not command contact: in the MPC the phase determined the contact schedule handed to the QP, whereas here the contact half is merely where the generator holds the foot at its lowest point, and contact is a consequence of that geometry. The paper words it as a wish, not a constraint: the legs should "engage ground contact in contact phase" (p. 8). The phase enters the policy's input as \langle\cos\phi_i, \sin\phi_i\rangle rather than as \phi_i (p. 8, Table S4: eight numbers for four legs). The reason is a discontinuity that is not physical. The leg's state is continuous through the end of a cycle, but the number \phi_i jumps from almost 2\pi to 0 . A network fed the raw angle sees two nearly identical situations as maximally different inputs, and has to learn that 0 and 2\pi mean the same thing. The pair \langle\cos\phi, \sin\phi\rangle is continuous in \phi and one-to-one onto the unit circle, so the same leg state always produces the same input and neighbouring leg states produce neighbouring inputs. This is the standard way to hand an angle to a network; the paper's phrase for it is "a smooth and unique representation for the angle." phase-and-ftg.svg Left: one phase per leg, the contact and swing halves, and why the pair \langle\cos\phi, \sin\phi\rangle is fed to the network while the raw angle is not. Right: the vertical foot target produced by the generator over one cycle (S3, eq. 11), with the residual the policy can add. When the operator gives the zero command for half a second, f_0 is set to 0 : the phases stop advancing, the generators hold the feet down, and the robot stands still. It restarts at 1.25\ \mathrm{Hz} when a direction command arrives or when the base is pushed faster than 0.3\ \mathrm{m/s} (S2). This small state machine lives inside the training environment, so the policy learns to stand and to walk under the same controller. S3 · The foot trajectory generator The generator is a function F(\phi): [0, 2\pi) \to \mathbb{R}^3 from phase to a nominal foot position in the horizontal frame H_i . The supplement's eq. (11) gives only a vertical component, along {}^{H_i}z : F(\phi_i) = \begin{cases} \big(h(-2k^3 + 3k^2) - 0.5\big)\, {}^{H_i}z & k \in [0, 1] \\[2pt] \big(h(2k^3 - 9k^2 + 12k - 4) - 0.5\big)\, {}^{H_i}z & k \in [1, 2] \\[2pt] 0.5\, {}^{H_i}z & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \qquad k = \frac{2(\phi_i - \pi)}{\pi}, \quad h = 0.2\ \mathrm{m}. Read it in three pieces. During the contact half ($k All forward progress comes from the residuals. The policy is not correcting a walking motion; it is turning a stepping motion into walking by adding lateral offsets that the generator knows nothing about. This is why the residuals are 12-dimensional and the frequencies are the only other output: the generator supplies timing and clearance, the policy supplies placement. p.8 · The horizontal frame The generator's output and the residuals are expressed in a frame H_i attached under the hip of leg i at the nominal reach. Its z -axis is parallel to the gravity vector e_g and its x -axis is the projection of the base's x -axis onto the horizontal plane. So H_i turns with the robot's yaw but ignores its roll and pitch (p. 8, from Barasuol et al. 2013). The nominal reach is the leg's hip-to-foot distance in the default standing configuration, not the fully extended length, so the origin of H_i sits at the default foothold of leg i : a zero residual leaves the foot where it rests in stance. The origin, though, does none of the work this section credits to the frame. Only the orientation gives the level prior, and a constant translation of the origin is indistinguishable from a constant bias in the residual, which training absorbs; the inverse kinematics needs the hip's position in the base frame in any case. What the choice buys is an action space in which zero means neutral and, because the frame is per-leg, the same residual means the same displacement on all four legs. Where exactly does the origin of H_i sit, and does it matter? → Lee 2020 - Learning Quadrupedal Locomotion over Challenging Terrain › Questions while reading Why this matters is easiest to see by imagining the alternative. If foot targets were expressed in the base frame, a pitched base would drag the nominal stepping motion with it: the generator would push feet into the ground on one side and lift them into the air on the other whenever the body tilted, and the policy would have to cancel the tilt with residuals before it could do anything else. In H_i the prior stays level no matter what the base does, so the residuals only have to handle terrain. The paper's summary is that the frame "reduces the effect of base attitude on the foot motions and consequently stabilizes training" (p. 8). You have used this frame under another name. The convex MPC of Di Carlo 2018 and the foothold planner in your article both rotate by yaw only, R_z(\psi) , and treat roll and pitch as disturbances to be corrected rather than as part of the reference geometry (Convex MPC for Legged Locomotion). H_i is the same choice applied to foot targets. horizontal-frame.svg A level base and a pitched base. The base frame B (red) tilts with the body; the horizontal frame H_i (blue) keeps only the yaw, so the same target coordinates in H_i put the foot at the same place relative to the ground. The bracket is the paper's nominal reach: the hip-to-foot distance in the default standing configuration, not the fully extended leg. The origin of H_i is at its lower end, so in stance the foot is at the origin. The figure draws the foot below the origin instead, copying eq. (11) literally; that is the one thing in it not to read as a distance. Two consequences the paper draws from the frame. Converting a target from H_i to the base frame requires the roll and pitch of the base, which is exactly the information the IMU's gravity vector provides (Sensors vs Simulator in Robot RL); yaw is not needed, and the IMU cannot give it anyway. Because {}^{H_i}z is aligned with gravity, "lateral" and "vertical" are separate coordinates of the residual, and the stochastic policy's exploration noise can be shaped per direction: larger noise laterally, "to promote exploration along the ground surface" (p. 8). That sentence is only meaningful once you know that the exploration noise of a Gaussian policy is a standard deviation per action coordinate, which is where §2 begins. p.8 · Analytic inverse kinematics Each target foot position is expressed in H_i , rotated into the base frame, and converted to three joint angles by closed-form inverse kinematics. Those joint targets are then tracked by the joint PD controllers at 400\ \mathrm{Hz} (Fig. 4C), through the actuator net in simulation and the real actuators on the robot. An ANYmal leg has three joints: hip abduction/adduction (HAA), hip flexion/extension (HFE), and knee flexion/extension (KFE). The inverse problem decouples into two planar problems. In the frontal plane, the lateral offset of the target fixes the HAA angle by a single arctangent. In the plane of the leg, the remaining two joints form a two-link chain, and the law of cosines gives the knee angle from the hip-to-foot distance d ; the hip pitch follows from the direction of the target and the interior angle at the hip. Two configurations satisfy the same target, knee forward and knee backward, and the implementation fixes one. leg-analytic-ik.svg Textbook version of the leg's inverse kinematics. Left: the hip roll angle from the frontal plane. Right: hip pitch and knee angle from the sagittal plane, with the second solution dashed. The real ANYmal leg has a few fixed offsets between joint axes that add terms but not ideas. The paper gives two reasons for analytic rather than numerical inverse kinematics (p. 8): computational efficiency, since the tracking loop runs at 400\ \mathrm{Hz} on an onboard CPU, and "to reuse existing position control actuator models for the sim-to-real transfer." The second reason is the deeper one. The actuator net of Hwangbo 2019 was trained on position-control data: joint position error and velocity in, torque out. By ending in joint position targets, this paper reuses the entire tracking stack, the PD law and the learned actuator, without touching it. Whatever the network does upstream, the part of the system that had been validated against hardware stays as it was. There is also a reason not to skip the foot-space detour and let the network output joint targets directly, and it is the same reason the prior exists at all. Write the leg's forward kinematics as p_f = k(q) , the foot position as a function of the three joint angles, and differentiate: \Delta p_f = J(q)\, \Delta q, \qquad J(q) = \frac{\partial k}{\partial q} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \Delta q = J(q)^{-1}\, \Delta p_f . Everything follows from the argument of J : the request in foot space is a constant, the answer in joint space is configuration-dependent. "Lift the foot two centimetres" is \Delta p_f = (0, 0, 0.02) whatever the leg happens to be doing, while the \Delta q that delivers it is a different triple of numbers for every q — small with the leg crouched, large near full extension, where J is ill-conditioned in the vertical direction. So there is no fixed map from phase to joint angles that means "a 20\ \mathrm{cm} swing": the same joint trajectory would trace a different foot path every time the posture changed. That is why eq. (11) can be one cubic in one coordinate, and why the per-direction exploration noise of p.8 · The horizontal frame is definable at all — joint space has no axis called lateral. The generator and the network work in the space where the geometry is trivial, and the conversion is charged to the inverse kinematics once per step. Gaussian policies: exploration is a standard deviation For a continuous action, the standard policy class is a Gaussian whose mean is the network output, \pi_\theta(a \mid s) = \mathcal{N}\big(a;\ \mu_\theta(s),\ \Sigma\big), \qquad \Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^2, \dots, \sigma_{16}^2). The network computes \mu_\theta(s) , a 16-vector of frequencies and residuals. The standard deviations are separate parameters, learned or scheduled, one per action coordinate. Sampling a \sim \pi_\theta during training is the exploration; at deployment the mean is used and the controller is deterministic. The score function for the mean is \nabla_\mu \log \pi = \Sigma^{-1}(a - \mu) , which is L7's Gaussian policy slide (Silver RL Lecture 7 - Lecture Notes › p.17–18 · Softmax and Gaussian Policies ⏱ 36:49): actions that came out above the mean and turned out well push the mean up. Now the sentence from §1 reads plainly. "We applied larger noise in the lateral direction" (p. 8) means \sigma is larger for the x and y components of the residuals than for z . That is only a well-defined choice because the residuals live in H_i , where z is along gravity. The stated aim is "to promote exploration along the ground surface" (p. 8): lateral exploration tries different footholds, which is where the terrain problem lives. Why a step size in parameter space is the wrong knob Vanilla policy gradient updates \theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha\, \hat g with a learning rate \alpha measured in parameter space. The problem is that the same \lVert\Delta\theta\rVert can be a negligible or a catastrophic change in behaviour, depending on where the policy currently is. The Gaussian makes this concrete. Shift the mean of \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) by \Delta\mu . The Kullback–Leibler divergence between old and new policy is D_{KL}\big(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\,\big\ \,\mathcal{N}(\mu + \Delta\mu, \sigma^2)\big) = \frac{\Delta\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}, so the same parameter step \Delta\mu = 0.5 is a divergence of 0.125 when \sigma = 1 and of 12.5 when \sigma = 0.1 . In the second case almost every action the new policy samples would have been essentially impossible under the old one. As training narrows \sigma , a fixed learning rate turns into ever larger policy changes, exactly when the policy has become good and has the most to lose. Two things go wrong when a step changes the policy too much. The gradient estimate was computed from the old policy's data and is a local statement; far from \theta_k it says nothing, so the step may make things worse. And a locomotion policy that has been made worse generates worse data (short episodes, falls), from which recovery is slow. This is the failure people call performance collapse, and avoiding it is the entire motivation for measuring the step in the space of behaviours rather than of parameters. trpo-kl-vs-euclidean.svg Left: the same mean shift is a small or a huge change of the action distribution depending on \sigma . Right: in parameter space, a ball of constant KL divergence is an ellipse whose shape depends on the current policy; TRPO takes the largest step inside it, which is the natural-gradient direction F^{-1} g . The TRPO problem and its guarantee TRPO (Schulman et al. 2015) replaces the learning rate by a constraint. Let \theta_k be the current parameters and \rho_{\theta_k} the state distribution the current policy visits. The surrogate objective is L_{\theta_k}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_k},\ a \sim \pi_{\theta_k}}\!\left[\frac{\pi_\theta(a \mid s)}{\pi_{\theta_k}(a \mid s)}\, A_{\theta_k}(s, a)\right], and the update is the solution of \max_\theta\ L_{\theta_k}(\theta) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \bar D_{KL}(\theta_k, \theta) := \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \rho_{\theta_k}}\!\Big[D_{KL}\big(\pi_{\theta_k}(\cdot \mid s)\,\big\ \,\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid s)\big)\Big] \le \delta. Three things to see in the surrogate. 1. The ratio \pi_\theta / \pi_{\theta_k} is an importance weight: the actions were sampled from the old policy, and the ratio re-weights them to evaluate the new one, exactly the one-step ratio of Importance Sampling in Off-Policy RL. 2. The states, by contrast, are not re-weighted; they stay distributed as under the old policy, which is an approximation that is accurate only while the two policies are close. 3. At \theta = \theta_k the ratio is 1 , so L_{\theta_k}(\theta_k) = 0 (the advantage has zero mean) and \nabla_\theta L_{\theta_k}\big _{\theta_k} = \mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta \cdot A] , the policy gradient of L7. To first order the surrogate is the L7 objective; it differs in how far from \theta_k it is trusted. The reason to trust it inside a KL ball is a theorem (Schulman et al. 2015, Theorem 1, building on Kakade and Langford 2002). For any two policies, J(\pi_\theta) \;\ge\; J(\pi_{\theta_k}) + L_{\theta_k}(\theta) - C \cdot D_{KL}^{\max}(\theta_k, \theta), \qquad C = \frac{4\epsilon\gamma}{(1 - \gamma)^2}, \quad \epsilon = \max_{s, a}\,\lvert A_{\theta_k}(s, a)\rvert, where D_{KL}^{\max} is the largest per-state divergence. The right-hand side equals J(\pi_{\theta_k}) at \theta = \theta_k . So maximising the right-hand side and moving to its maximiser can never lower J : it is a lower bound that touches the objective at the current point, and pushing the bound up pushes the objective up with it. This argument, maximise a touching lower bound, is the minorisation–maximisation pattern, and it is the correctness bridge between the surrogate and the true return. Two approximations separate the theorem from the algorithm, and both are worth stating precisely because the guarantee does not survive them unchanged. The penalty coefficient C is enormous for \gamma near 1 , so maximising the penalised bound would produce steps too small to be useful; TRPO therefore replaces the penalty by the hard constraint \bar D_{KL} \le \delta with \delta a tuned hyperparameter. And the theorem's D_{KL}^{\max} over all states cannot be estimated from samples, so the constraint uses the mean KL over visited states instead. With those two substitutions the monotonic-improvement guarantee becomes a heuristic that works well in practice, not a theorem. From the constrained problem to the update rule The constrained problem cannot be solved exactly for a network with on the order of 10^5 parameters (the student networks in Table S6 have about 1.6 \times 10^5 ; the teacher is of the same order), so TRPO solves a local approximation of it and then checks the result. Linearise the objective and quadratise the constraint around \theta_k : L_{\theta_k}(\theta) \approx g^\top (\theta - \theta_k), \qquad \bar D_{KL}(\theta_k, \theta) \approx \tfrac12\, (\theta - \theta_k)^\top F\, (\theta - \theta_k), where g is the policy gradient estimate and F is the Hessian of the mean KL at \theta_k , which is the Fisher information matrix F = \mathbb{E}\big[\nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta\, \nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta^{\top}\big] . The first-order objective under a quadratic constraint has a closed-form maximiser: \Delta\theta = \sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{g^\top F^{-1} g}}\ F^{-1} g . The direction F^{-1} g is the natural gradient of L7's skipped slides (Silver RL Lecture 7 - Lecture Notes › Gaps to close on your own): the steepest direction when distance is measured by KL rather than by the Euclidean norm on \theta . The scalar in front is the step length that lands exactly on the boundary \bar D_{KL} = \delta under the quadratic approximation. The obstacle is F . For 10^5 parameters it has 10^{10} entries; it can be neither stored nor inverted. TRPO never forms it. It solves F x = g with the conjugate gradient method, which only needs the product F v for a given vector v , and that product is available by automatic differentiation of the KL at the cost of a few backward passes per iteration. A small multiple of the identity is added, (F + \lambda I)\, x = g , so that the system is well-posed when F is nearly singular; this \lambda is the "CG damping" of Table S7. Ten to fifty iterations give a good enough x \approx F^{-1} g . Finally, because both approximations can be off, the full step is checked against the real quantities: a backtracking line search shrinks \Delta\theta by a constant factor until the sampled mean KL is at most \delta and the sampled surrogate has actually improved. That check is what makes the method robust in practice: the approximations propose, the constraint decides. What TRPO does not guarantee The theorem bounds the true return using the maximum per-state KL; the algorithm constrains the mean. The theorem's penalty is replaced by a constraint whose \delta is tuned. The Fisher matrix is estimated from the same batch as the gradient. Each of these is standard, and each is a place where the guarantee is no longer a guarantee. The ablation in Fig. 5E–G shows the same thing under controlled conditions: a TCN-20 trained by TRPO on proprioception alone, with the teacher's reward and hyperparameters, never learns to balance (short episodes, low reward), while the same architecture trained by imitation of a privileged teacher does. Read "sparse" as a statement about how much the signal says, not about how often it arrives; a reward arrives every step. This reading is mine, not the paper's, but it is what the ablation supports. One scalar per step, mixing seven objectives, has to teach a network both what to extract from a two-second history (is a foot trapped? is the ground sloping? was I pushed?) and what to do about it. The two problems are coupled: the network cannot learn what to extract until it knows what matters for acting, and cannot learn to act well until it extracts the right things. Privileged learning breaks the coupling by solving the second problem first, with the answer to the first handed over as input. The pattern comes from learning by cheating (Chen et al. 2019), where an agent with access to the ground-truth layout of a driving scene is trained first, and a second agent that sees only camera images is trained to imitate it. This paper's variation is that the privileged agent is trained by RL rather than from human demonstrations, because nobody can demonstrate ANYmal over rough terrain. lee2020-fig4-highlight-a.png Fig. 4 (p. 7), panel A highlighted. Step 1: the teacher is trained by policy gradient with the privileged information x_t as part of its input. Step 2: the student, with a proprioceptive history in place of x_t , is trained to reproduce both the teacher's latent \bar l_t and its action \bar a_t . The head layers are copied. p.8 · Privileged information: what the teacher is allowed to know Table S4 lists the privileged block x_t : the terrain normal at each foot, the elevation of nine scan points on a 10\ \mathrm{cm} circle around each foot, foot contact forces and states, thigh and shank contact states, the friction coefficient under each foot, and the external force applied to the base during training. Every one of these is a hidden cause of something the student will see in proprioception: a slipping foot, an unexpected stop of a descending leg, a base that accelerates without the legs having done anything. The rule of Sensors vs Simulator in Robot RL is that an observation must be measurable on the robot. That rule was stated for a policy that deploys. The teacher does not deploy, so its observation may contain simulator-only quantities, exactly as the reward always could. The split between what is allowed in the reward and what is allowed in the observation has moved: for the teacher, both lists are the simulator's. The teacher does not consume x_t raw. An encoder compresses it into a 64-dimensional latent \bar l_t (Table S5: \tanh(72) \to \tanh(64) ), and the action head takes \bar l_t together with o_t . The command and the robot's own state are deliberately kept out of x_t , so that \bar l_t "contains only the terrain- and contact-related features" (p. 8). That bottleneck is a design choice made for the student's sake: it produces a compact, well-defined target for what the student's history must encode, "what the ground is doing", in 64 numbers. p.9 · Behavior cloning is regression, and where it breaks Imitation learning in its simplest form is supervised regression. Given a dataset \mathcal{D} of input–label pairs (z, a^) , where a^ is the expert's action at that input, fit a policy by minimising the squared error over the dataset. The paper's student loss is this, with two labels (eq. 1): \mathcal{L} = \big\lVert \bar a_t(o_t, x_t) - a_t(o_t, H)\big\rVert^2 + \big\lVert \bar l_t(o_t, x_t) - l_t(H)\big\rVert^2 . Bars are the teacher's outputs, computed with the privileged x_t ; unbarred are the student's, computed from the history H . Compared with RL, this is an easy problem for two reasons. The supervision is dense: eighty numbers per step, sixteen action components and sixty-four latent components, each with a definite target, instead of one scalar. And there is no credit assignment across time: each step is its own regression problem. The catch is the distribution the regression is accurate on. A regressor is accurate on inputs like those it was trained on. If \mathcal{D} is collected by running the teacher, the student learns to be accurate on the states the teacher visits. But the student is not the teacher. Its small errors move it to states slightly off the teacher's distribution, where it was trained less and errs more, which moves it further off, where it errs more still. This is covariate shift, and in sequential decision-making it compounds: Ross and Bagnell (2010) show that a per-step imitation error of \epsilon on the training distribution can cost O(T^2 \epsilon) over a horizon of T steps, because one mistake can put the learner in unfamiliar states for the rest of the episode. Plain behavior cloning of a locomotion teacher would produce a student that walks well for a moment and then falls in ways the teacher never did. dagger-covariate-shift.svg Left: behavior cloning trains only on the teacher's states. Middle: at test time the student's own errors take it where no labels exist, and they compound. Right: DAgger rolls out the student and asks the teacher for labels at the student's own states, so the next student is trained where it actually goes. p.9 · DAgger: label where the student goes DAgger, dataset aggregation (Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell 2011), fixes the distribution by changing who generates the states. Iterate: run the current student and record the states it visits; ask the expert for its action at each of those states; add these pairs to the aggregate dataset; retrain the student on everything collected so far. The original algorithm mixes expert and student control in early iterations with a decaying probability \beta_i ; the essential step is that the labels are collected on the student's state distribution. Under a no-regret learner, the returned policy's cost is O(T\epsilon) plus regret terms rather than O(T^2\epsilon) (Ross et al. 2011, Section 3, Theorems 3.1–3.2). The paper's description is one sentence and is exactly this: "training data is generated by rolling out trajectories by the student policy. For each visited state, the teacher policy computes its embedding and action vectors" (p. 9). Notice what DAgger requires of the expert. It must answer "what would you do here?" at arbitrary states chosen by the student, not just at states on its own trajectories. A dataset of human demonstrations cannot do that. A teacher that runs in the simulator can, trivially: at whatever state the student has reached, the physics engine supplies x_t , the teacher network is evaluated, and the labels \bar l_t, \bar a_t are written down. This is the second reason privileged learning and DAgger belong together, and it is another consequence of the tip in The one idea. Once the student is trained on its own state distribution, there is no shift between training and test in simulation. The remaining shift is between simulation and the robot, and DAgger does nothing about that one. It is addressed, as in Hwangbo 2019, by randomising dynamics and friction, adding observation noise and pushes, and by the actuator net (S2). p.9, S9 · Why imitate the latent, and why copy the head Two design details make the student's job easier and are easy to miss. The action head of the student is not trained from scratch. Table S5 marks the layers \tanh(256) \to \tanh(128) \to \tanh(64) \to output as copied from the teacher after teacher training. If the student's encoder produced l_t = \bar l_t exactly, the copied head would produce \bar a_t exactly. So the two loss terms are consistent by construction: the latent term teaches the encoder what to extract from the history, and the action term corrects whatever the latent term leaves. Imitation mostly trains the new part, the encoder. The latent term matters. S9 ablates it: a student trained on the action term alone ("naive IL") matches on slopes and under pushes but has a lower success rate on steps. The reading is that the action target alone tells the encoder only what is needed to reproduce actions on the training distribution, while the latent target says explicitly which sixty-four features about the ground to recover, a denser and more direct supervision of the representation. It can only recover what the history predicts. Terrain that has not yet been touched leaves no trace in proprioception, which is why the paper's Discussion calls the gait "fairly conservative since it must by necessity feel out the environment with its body as it locomotes" (p. 6), and why the paper points to a hybrid proprioceptive–exteroceptive controller as future work. 4 · Memory: partial observability and the TCN 🔴 for the partial-observability argument and causal 1-D convolution · ⚪ for the recurrent alternative p.8–9 · Why the student needs a history The student sees o_t and not x_t . Everything in x_t still affects what happens next, so the student's observation is not a Markov state: the same o_t can occur with a foot about to hit a step or on flat ground, on ice or on rubber, pushed or not pushed. In RL vocabulary the student faces a partially observable problem, a POMDP (Silver L1; the POMDP slides of L2 were skipped, but the aliased gridworld of Silver RL Lecture 7 - Lecture Notes › p.7–9 · Aliased Gridworld ⏱ 15:25 is the same failure in miniature: identical observations in different situations). A policy that reacts to o_t alone must react identically in situations that call for different actions. There are three standard cures. 1. The exact one: the belief state, the posterior over the hidden variables given the whole history, which converts the POMDP into an MDP over beliefs; it is exact and intractable here. 2. The second: feed a window of recent observations and let the network compute whatever statistic of it is useful. 3. The third: a recurrent network that carries a state forward. The paper takes the second cure with a window of N = 100 observations at 0.02\ \mathrm{s} , two seconds, and states its hypothesis on p. 8: the teacher's latent \bar l_t "can be (partially) recovered from a time series of proprioceptive observations." The word partially is honest: the history predicts what has been touched, not what lies ahead. Why should hidden causes be recoverable from proprioception at all? Because they leave traces. A foot that hits a step stops descending early: a jump in position error and a drop in velocity in that leg's joints. A foot that slips moves while the leg is in stance. A push changes the base velocity without any leg having done anything to cause it. Terrain height is where the foot stopped. Hwangbo 2019 already exploited this with a history of two samples, as its substitute for a contact sensor (Sensors vs Simulator in Robot RL › Contact detection without a force sensor); this paper extends the same idea to a hundred samples and lets the network decide what to extract. How much history is needed is an empirical question, and the paper answers it in Fig. 5B–D. On a uniform slope, one sample is enough; the slope is visible in the gravity vector at every instant. On a step, memory decides: the hind legs have to clear a step that only the front legs have touched, a second or more earlier at walking speed, and short-memory controllers fail there. Under a lateral push, the two-second controller deviates about a third less than the one-sample controller. Three quantities are dropped from the student's per-step input h_t (p. 9): the base frequency, the joint history, and the previous foot targets. All three were short-hand histories inside o_t , and they are redundant once the window itself is the input. The DSP view: a causal 1-D convolution is an FIR filter with learned taps The student's encoder is a temporal convolutional network, TCN (Bai, Kolter, and Koltun 2018). You know its building block under another name. A one-dimensional convolution over time with filter size K , y[t] = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} w_k\, x[t - k], is a finite impulse response filter: K taps, applied to the current and past samples, the same taps at every t . The only difference from Signals & Systems is that the taps w_k are learned by gradient descent rather than designed. With many input channels (the 60 proprioceptive signals of h_t ) and many output channels, each output channel is a sum over input channels of such filters: a filter bank with channel mixing. A ReLU after each layer makes the stack nonlinear, so the whole network is not an LTI system, but each layer's linear part is. Causal: the output at t uses no samples after t , which is what makes the network runnable in real time, one output per new sample. Dilated: a layer with dilation d places its taps d samples apart, y[t] = \sum_k w_k\, x[t - k d] , so that stacking dilations 1, 2, 4 multiplies the span the output sees while the number of taps grows only linearly. Strided: a stride- 2 layer keeps every second output, which is decimation by two; the sequence gets shorter and the layers after it cheaper. tcn-dilated-causal-conv.svg Top: one causal 1-D convolution is an FIR filter whose taps are learned. Bottom: stacking layers with dilations 1, 2, 4 grows the span of the input the final output can see; only the blue connections feed that output. For a stack of layers with filter size K and dilations d_\ell , all with stride 1 , the receptive field is R = 1 + (K - 1)\sum_{\ell} d_\ell . A stride- 2 layer doubles the input spacing of every layer after it, so the same formula applies with each later d_\ell multiplied by the accumulated stride. S8 · The recurrent alternative, as an anchor A gated recurrent unit keeps a state, h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t) , that in principle summarises the entire past; in filter language it is closer to an IIR recursion than to an FIR window. It is trained by backpropagation through time, and truncated BPTT limits how far back the gradient is propagated, for cost and stability. The paper's only reason for using it instead of the reward is that it found traversability "more intuitive than the reward function", which consists of multiple objectives that are often unbounded (p. 9). The ingredient is a label on each state transition (eq. 2), \nu(s_t, a_t, s_{t+1}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } v_{pr}(s_{t+1}) > 0.2 \\ 0 & \text{if } v_{pr}(s_{t+1}) "neither too easy nor too difficult" (p. 9). Desirability is defined as (eqs. 4–5) \mathrm{Td}(c_T, \pi) := \Pr\big(\mathrm{Tr}(c_T, \pi) \in [0.5, 0.9]\big) = \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \pi}\big\{\mathbb{1}\big(\mathrm{Tr}(c_T, \pi) \in [0.5, 0.9]\big)\big\}, where 0.5 and 0.9 are fixed minimum and maximum thresholds. The indicator is missing from eq. 5 as printed (p. 9); it is restored here from eqs. 7 and 10. The \mathrm{Tr} inside the probability is the traversability of a single trajectory, a random quantity; \mathrm{Td} is the probability that it lands in the band. Read against eq. 3 alone, \mathrm{Tr}(c_T, \pi) is one number and \Pr(\mathrm{Tr} \in [0.5, 0.9]) could only be 0 or 1 . Eq. 5 takes the expectation over \xi \sim \pi , and eq. 7 below counts trajectories, so the indicator is applied trajectory by trajectory. The paper does not write the single-trajectory \mathrm{Tr} out; the reading consistent with eq. 3 is the fraction of that trajectory's transitions with \nu = 1 . It also does not say why it thresholds each trajectory rather than the pooled rate. What makes two trajectories on the same c_T differ is not discussed as such. Desirability \mathrm{Td} is the probability that this indicator equals 1 for a trajectory (eqs. 4–5), so it can take any value in [0, 1] . Two labels are the figure's, not the paper's: "nothing left to learn" on the easy side, and the footnote's pooling of transitions over all trajectories, whereas eq. 7 applies the indicator to each trajectory's \mathrm{Tr} . Desirability becomes a measurement model through a binary variable (p. 9): y^k_j = 1 if \mathrm{Tr}(c^k_{T,j}, \pi) \in [0.5, 0.9] . Then (eq. 6) \Pr\big(y^k_j \mid c^k_{T,j}\big) = \Pr\big(\mathrm{Tr}(c^k_{T,j}, \pi) \in [0.5, 0.9]\big) = \mathrm{Td}\big(c^k_{T,j}, \pi\big). The middle term is printed with c^k_{T,i} , a typo for c^k_{T,j} . What you need is a two-valued measurement model and the likelihood: read with c varying, \mathrm{Td}(c, \pi) is the likelihood of y = 1 , not a distribution over c . Only this y = 1 value is ever computed (eq. 6, Algorithm S1 line 14); no y = 0 enters a weight. In practice the measurement probability is the empirical expectation over the samples collected during policy training (eq. 7): \Pr\big(y^k_j \mid c^k_{T,j}\big) \approx \sum^{N_{traj}} \frac{\mathbb{1}\big(\mathrm{Tr}(c^k_{T,j}, \pi) \in [0.5, 0.9]\big)}{N_{traj}}, where N_{traj} is the number of trajectories generated using c^k_{T,j} (the sum is printed without a lower index). "The trajectories are also used for policy training," so the curriculum needs no additional evaluation steps (p. 9). S2 then slows the update: the curriculum is updated every N_{evaluate} policy iterations "to reduce variance," assuming the policy's performance is similar within that window, and the estimate becomes (eq. 10) \Pr\big(y^k_j \mid c^k_{T,j}\big) \approx \sum^{N_{evaluate}} \sum^{N_{traj}} \frac{\mathbb{1}\big(\mathrm{Tr}(c^k_{T,j}, \pi) \in [0.5, 0.9]\big)}{N_{traj}\, N_{evaluate}} . \mathrm{Tr} is judged per trajectory, and the measurement probability is the in-band fraction pooled over N_{traj} \times N_{evaluate} = 6 \times 10 = 60 trajectories per particle per curriculum update (Table S3). How noisy is that fraction? If the 60 in-band indicators were independent Bernoulli trials with a common p , their count would be binomial with variance 60\,p(1-p) , so the fraction would have standard deviation \sqrt{p(1-p)/60} , at most 0.065 , against at most 0.205 from N_{traj} = 6 alone. That is my arithmetic, consistent with the direction of the paper's stated reason. The window guarantees neither independence nor a common p : the policy is updated ten times inside it, and the paper assumes, rather than shows, that its performance stays similar. Without a common p the fraction estimates the window average of \mathrm{Td} rather than \mathrm{Td} for one policy; without independence, since later policies are trained on earlier trajectories, the standard deviation can exceed the bound. p.9 · What is filtered: the textbook particle filter, piece by piece The paper says its algorithm is "modeled on the Sequential Importance Resampling (SIR) particle filter" (p. 9). Its target is the distribution of terrain parameters that satisfy \mathrm{Tr}(c_T, \pi) \in [0.5, 0.9] , and the set of tuples \langle c^k_T, w^k\rangle , k = 1, \dots, N_{particle} , "approximates the target distribution." In the lectures' sense a weighted particle set approximates a distribution when its weighted averages match expectations, not density values point by point. The tracked quantity is not a hidden physical state. It is a distribution over terrain parameters, concentrated where terrains are desirable for the current policy. It changes during training because \mathrm{Td}(c_T, \pi) has the policy as an argument, not because terrains have dynamics. Terrain parameters with similar \mathrm{Tr}(\cdot, \pi) are close in Euclidean distance in parameter space. Source: the insight that terrain parameters can be interpolated; for example, a staircase gets harder as the step height increases. 2. A policy trained on terrains from some area of \mathcal{C} learns to interpolate to nearby terrain parameters. The paper does not link assumption 1 to the random walk; its only support is the interpolation example. For assumption 3, what you need is the full-form Markov assumption. Algorithm S1 · One iteration of sequential importance resampling Algorithm S1 (p. 15) is titled "Teacher training with automatic terrain curriculum." Condensed, with the paper's line numbers and loop nesting: ```text 1 init replay memory; N_particle c_T,0 ~ U(C); i, j = 0 2 repeat 3 for 0 One curriculum update spans N_{evaluate} policy updates. Lines 3–12 are ordinary teacher training. For each particle, N_{traj} episodes are run on terrains generated from that particle's value, each with the robot at a random position, and every transition is labelled by eq. 2. The TRPO update of §2 sits inside the k loop, after the rollouts of all particles, so each policy update consumes trajectories from every particle's terrain. That is the paper's "no additional evaluation steps": the rollouts that train the policy are the ones the curriculum scores. Table S3 counts 10 particles per terrain type; the paper does not say whether the types form separate filters or how their rollouts are combined into one TRPO batch. The window of N_{evaluate} policy updates exists "to reduce variance," under the assumption that the policy's performance is similar within it (S2). Lines 13–14 compute each particle's measurement probability. The printed reference "Eq. 9" is a typo: eq. 9 is the saliency map on p. 12, and the formula that pools over k and m , matching these loops, is eq. 10. Lines 15–16 compute the weights, printed as w_j = \frac{P\big(y^l_i \mid c^l_{T,j}\big)}{\sum_m P\big(y^m_i \mid c^m_{T,j}\big)} . The weight carries no particle index l , and y carries the policy counter i where eq. 6 writes y^k_j ; read both as notation slips. What matters is the structure: the weight is recomputed each cycle from the current measurement probability alone, with no previous-weight factor. The normalisation is the sum in the denominator (self-normalisation). Why that is consistent, which the paper does not explain: line 17 resamples in every cycle, so the particles entering the next weighting carry equal weights. Without resampling the weight would be the product w_t \propto w_{t-1}\, p(y_t \mid x_t) ; after resampling at every step, w_{t-1} = 1/N is absorbed into the proportionality, and the weight is the likelihood under the transition used as the proposal. The lectures assume the likelihood is evaluated exactly at each particle. Here it is a random fraction, and two consequences have no lecture behind them. The weights inherit the estimate's noise. If the policy were fixed over the window, the fraction would be an unbiased, non-negative estimate of \mathrm{Td} ; independence of the trajectories matters for its variance, not its mean. Particle filters that put such estimates into the weights go by the name random-weight particle filters, and the lectures do not cover them. A particle whose 60 trajectories all fall outside the band gets weight 0 and cannot survive resampling. Under the same independence assumption, a terrain with \mathrm{Td} = 0.02 would be estimated at 0 with probability 0.98^{60} \approx 0.30 (my arithmetic). If normalisation is per terrain type (not stated) and every particle of a type scores 0 , the denominator of line 16 is 0 ; if it is pooled over all types, a type whose particles all score 0 loses them all at resampling, and the denominator is 0 only when every particle of every type scores 0 . The paper addresses neither case. Line 17 resamples N_{particle} parameters, choosing the k th with probability equal to its normalised weight (p. 9). What you need is the categorical draw and its random copy counts: resampling draws from the weighted particle set, not from the target itself. It runs unconditionally; there is no effective-sample-size test. Its costs are the lectures' impoverishment (duplicated values after resampling) and deprivation (no particles left in a region that matters). On a discrete grid such as \mathcal{C} , duplicates are not a defect in themselves. Lines 18 and 20 are the replay memory. Line 18 appends c_{T,j} ; since it follows the resampling at line 17, the natural reading is the resampled set. Line 18 comes before line 20 samples from the memory, so the memory already includes the current cycle. The paper's entire rationale is one sentence: replay memory is used "to prevent degeneration of the particle filter and to avoid catastrophic forgetting" (S2). It gives no mechanism, no memory capacity, and does not say whether a particle drawn from the memory is also moved at line 21. Read against the lectures (my reading, not the paper's), a draw from the memory puts back a value the current weights did not select. That resembles the random-particle injection of L7 §5 with past particle values in place of random ones, and the lecture's conclusion about injection carries over: it lowers the risk of deprivation without removing it, and it changes the target. The paper also does not say which failure it calls "degeneration." Weight degeneracy accumulated over many cycles, as in L7 §2, cannot build up here, because line 16 keeps no weight history. Lines 19 and 21 are the transition. On p. 9 each parameter of a sampling point is shifted to its adjacent value with a fixed probability p_{transition} ; line 21 words the move per particle. Neither says whether coordinates move independently, which neighbour is chosen, how large a step is, or what happens at the bounds of \mathcal{C} . Terrain parameters have no dynamics of their own. Nothing in the simulator changes a particle's c_T between cycles, and resampling only copies values already in the set. Lines 20–21 are therefore the only way a value not in the current set can enter it. A replay draw can only restore a value that was in an earlier set; only the random walk can produce a value never visited before. Without them the parameter is static, and repeated resampling of a static parameter under multinomial resampling ends at a single value with probability 1 . The lecture warns that roughening adds noise that is not in the model and so changes the target; here, on my reading, there is no model to depart from, since the random walk is the transition model by definition. The paper gives no reason for choosing a random walk; it says only that the random walk satisfies assumption 3 (p. 9). The order of steps differs from the lectures' SIR cycle only in where it starts. Fig. 5 · Ablation logic, seeds, and intervals An ablation removes one component while holding the rest fixed and measures what is lost. Fig. 5 does this three times: history length N (B–D), privileged training versus direct RL (E–G), adaptive versus uniform terrains (H–J), each on three diagnostic tests, an omnidirectional slope, a discrete step, and a lateral push, with 100 trials per test. Every model was trained five times with different random seeds and the error bars are 95 % confidence intervals. Two sources of randomness are folded into those bars: the trials, whose success rate is a binomial proportion with standard error at most \sqrt{0.25/100} = 0.05 , and the training runs themselves, whose outcome varies with initialisation and sampling. Five seeds is the field's convention and is small; the Roadmap's Section 5 (Paper Reading Roadmap) lists the paper that shows why single-seed results are not results. Read Fig. 5 by asking whether the intervals overlap, not by the height of the bars. p.12 · The decoder probe: what the encoding contains, with an uncertainty To see what the student's history encoding holds, the paper trains a decoder after the fact, with the policy frozen, from an intermediate layer of the TCN back to the privileged information x_t . Discrete targets (contact states) use a cross-entropy loss. Continuous targets use a Gaussian negative log-likelihood in which the decoder predicts both a mean and a standard deviation per component (eq. 8): \mathcal{L} = \sum_i \left[\frac{\big(x_i^{gt} - \mu_i\big)^2}{2\sigma_i^2} + \log \sigma_i\right]. This is heteroscedastic regression (Kendall and Gal 2017). The first term punishes an error more when the network claims to be certain; the second punishes claiming uncertainty. Per sample the loss is minimised at \sigma_i = \lvert x_i^{gt} - \mu_i\rvert , so the predicted \sigma learns to track the actual error, and it can be read as the encoding's uncertainty. That is what Fig. 6B and Fig. S2 plot: the estimated elevation under the front feet rises when a foot hits a step, its uncertainty grows, and the uncertainty stays elevated afterwards on rough ground, which the paper reads as the encoding carrying terrain roughness. gaussian-nll-uncertainty.svg The two terms of the Gaussian negative log-likelihood pull in opposite directions and meet at \sigma = \lvert y - \mu\rvert . One caution on reading a probe. That x_t can be decoded from the features shows the information is present in them, not that the policy uses it. The saliency analysis is the paper's answer to the second question. p.12 · Saliency Eq. (9) defines the saliency of the i -th past measurement as M_i = \sum_{j \in \text{channels}} \left\lvert \frac{\partial\, (r_{f,T})_z}{\partial H_{i,j}} \right\rvert , the absolute sensitivity of the commanded foot height to each entry of the input window, summed over channels: one row of the input–output Jacobian in the sense of Matrix Calculus (Gradients) (Simonyan et al. 2013). Fig. 6C–D shows the saliency peaking at the moment the front foot hit the step and staying high through the following swing: the policy keeps attending to that one collision sample while it lifts the foot higher. Decoding showed the information was there; saliency shows it was used. p.5 · Cost of transport The paper's efficiency measure is the mechanical cost of transport, \mathrm{COT} = \frac{\sum_{\text{12 actuators}} [\tau_i \dot\theta_i]^{+}}{m\, g\, v}, $$ positive mechanical power only (negative work, when an actuator brakes, is excluded), divided by weight times speed. b: Slides: David Silver - RL Course (UCL 2015) · Previous: Silver RL Lecture 9 - Lecture Notes · Next: — (final lecture) First pass: read The one idea and the slide-group headings. Use the prose when an equation, condition, or figure needs explanation; leave Gaps to close for review. This is the lecture where the slides matter most, and the video shows them worst L10 is a case-study lecture: the payload is in tables, game positions, and search-tree diagrams, and the recording makes several of them hard to read. Everything below is embedded from the source PDF at full resolution, so the figures you could not make out in the video are legible here. The one idea Nine lectures built machinery. This one asks a single question: when people actually beat world champions, what did they use? — and the answer turns out to be one recipe, applied seven times. The final slide is the whole lecture: Input features Value fn RL Training Search Chess (Meep) binary linear TreeStrap self-play \alpha\beta Checkers (Chinook) binary linear TD leaf self-play \alpha\beta Othello (Logistello) binary linear MC self-play \alpha\beta Backgammon (TD-Gammon) binary neural net TD( \lambda ) self-play \alpha\beta / MC Go (MoGo) binary linear TD self-play MCTS Scrabble (Maven) binary linear MC self-play MC search Poker (SmooCT) binary linear MCTS self-play — Read the columns, not only the rows. A repeated pattern appears: compact binary features, often a linear value function, self-play, and search. The exact learning and search algorithms vary by game, and TD-Gammon's neural network is the clearest representation outlier. The recurring three-part recipe Self-play can supply the data without a fixed expert dataset, by letting the agent adapt to opponents that are also changing. A value function compresses what was learned into a position evaluation. Search recovers, at play time, the tactical precision the value function cannot represent. These are not logical necessities for every game — Deep Blue had no learning, and some table entries use little or no online search. They are the recurring empirical recipe behind the RL systems in this lecture. Nash equilibrium is a fixed point of self-play, which is why self-play is principled A best response to fixed opponents is an ordinary single-agent RL problem — push the opponents into the environment and solve the resulting MDP. A Nash equilibrium is the joint policy where everyone is simultaneously playing a best response. Self-play aims at that condition: each player's policy defines the other's environment, so improving one changes the problem the other faces. If every player is a best response at a fixed point, that fixed point is a Nash equilibrium. Reaching such a point is not automatic; naive best-response dynamics can cycle. That is the honest case for games: simple enough to iterate, deep enough to matter, and with a benchmark no other domain offers — humans who have spent their lives becoming the best possible at exactly this. Compare p.4 (all of AI) against p.5 (RL only) and read the overlap: five of seven games were first brought to their best-known level by reinforcement learning. The two exceptions are instructive rather than embarrassing — in chess RL reached International Master, well short of Deep Blue, and in poker there is now a superhuman RL method. That is the claim underwriting the rest of the lecture: RL is not one approach among many here. It is the primary mechanism by which classic games were solved. 2 · Game theory, minimally p.6–7 · Best Response and Nash Equilibrium ⏱ 7:41 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=7 In an MDP "optimal" is unambiguous. With another player it is not: the best policy against an opponent who always plays rock is to always play paper, and that policy is catastrophic against anyone else. Optimality has to be defined relative to what everyone else does, which is why the lecture needs game theory at all. Two concepts, and the second is the one that matters: Best response \pi^i_(\pi^{-i}) — the optimal policy against fixed opponents. Push them into the environment and it is an ordinary MDP. Nash equilibrium — a joint policy where every player is playing a best response to all the others. Nobody would choose to deviate. For rock-paper-scissors the Nash equilibrium is uniform random. Any deviation creates a regularity, and a regularity is exploitable. Is the Nash equilibrium unique? Not in general. In the two-player zero-sum setting, the minimax value is unique, but multiple policies can attain it; therefore equilibrium policies need not be unique even when the value is. The slide makes the precise claim: a minimax policy is a Nash equilibrium and the minimax value function is unique. Imperfect-information games such as poker can also have many equilibrium strategies. Section 8 needs different machinery primarily because players act from different information states, not merely because equilibria may be non-unique. The connection back to your own homework Easy21 fixed the dealer's policy and folded it into the environment — a best-response problem. If both sides learn and the process reaches an equilibrium, the result is a joint solution concept rather than a policy tailored to one fixed dealer. Convergence still depends on the particular multi-agent algorithm and its assumptions. The convergence question is deferred until ⏱ 1:24:33. Silver points to Littman's tabular minimax-RL results as evidence that convergence is possible for suitable algorithms and assumptions. Do not generalize this to arbitrary “standard RL under self-play”; everything practical in this lecture uses approximation or search outside that simple guarantee. p.8–9 · Zero-Sum and Perfect Information ⏱ 18:20 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=9 Two restrictions, each buying something concrete: Zero-sum ( R^1+R^2=0 ) means good-for-white is exactly bad-for-black, so one value function suffices — negate it for the other player's view. It also means the players are never partly cooperating, which is what makes minimax the right solution concept. Perfect information means fully observed. Note that this does not mean deterministic: backgammon has dice and is still perfect information, because you see the entire board state. The distinction is observability, not stochasticity — a confusion the slide's bullet list invites. 3 · Minimax search p.10–11 · The Minimax Value Function ⏱ 21:23 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=10 v_(s)=\max_{\pi^1}\min_{\pi^2}v_\pi(s) Read it as "if both players try their hardest against each other, who wins from here?" The \max\min notation compresses a nested alternation — white maximizes, then black minimizes, then white maximizes — down the whole sequence. It is shorthand for the tree, not a two-step operation. In the standard game setting there are no intermediate rewards: zero throughout, then a terminal outcome. If the payoff is 1 for a win and 0 otherwise, v_\pi(s)=\mathbb P(\text{win}\mid s) . With +1 for a win and -1 for a loss and no draws, v_\pi(s)=2\,\mathbb P(\text{win}\mid s)-1. So value is an affine transform of win probability, not literally the probability under every reward convention. Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=11 Minimax search dates to Claude Shannon's Programming a Computer for Playing Chess — the first chess program ever written, which ran on paper, because there was no computer to run it on. Most of the concepts still in use were already there. p.12–15 · The Worked Example ⏱ 27:29 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=15 Four slides animating one depth-first pass: evaluate the leaves, take maxima at Max's nodes, minima at Min's, and back up to the root, which comes out at -2 via a_1 . The thing to extract is not the arithmetic but the consequence: this computes the optimal policy, not just the optimal values. The backed-up choice at each node is the minimax policy. If you could run this to the end of the game you would be finished. You cannot, because the tree grows exponentially with depth. Everything after this slide is a response to that one fact. p.16–17 · Truncating the Search with a Value Function ⏱ 29:45 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=16 Search to a fixed depth, then call a function approximator at the leaves and back those values up instead of real outcomes. The evaluation function is a value function, and naming it correctly is the point Game-tree literature calls it an "evaluation function" or "heuristic function", which makes it sound like a domain-specific device. In this course's vocabulary it is exactly \hat v(s,\mathbf{w})\approx v_(s) — a value function approximator estimating the minimax value. Once you see that, the whole of L6 applies to it, and the rest of the lecture becomes "how do we learn these weights?" rather than "what heuristic should we hand-write?". Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=17 v(s,\mathbf{w})=x(s)\cdot\mathbf{w}=5+3-5=3 The binary-linear evaluation is the same construction from L6 p.15 — binary features, a weight per feature, and a dot product. What makes it fast is sparsity: you never touch the zero features; you sum the weights of the features that are present. Two extensions the slide does not mention. Piece-square tables condition a piece's value on where it sits, and modern programs use conjunctions of pieces and positions — a strong shogi program uses on the order of ten million such features. The construction does not change; only the feature count does. The resulting score need not be a calibrated win probability. A logistic output can enforce a probability-like range, but many game engines use an uncalibrated evaluation scale because search needs reliable ordering more than calibrated probabilities. p.18–19 · Deep Blue and Chinook ⏱ 35:48 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=18 Deep Blue contains no learning at all 8,000 handcrafted features with weights hand-tuned by a team of human grandmasters, plus 480 custom chess processors searching 200 million positions per second, 16–40 ply deep. It defeated Kasparov 4–2 in 1997. It is in this lecture as the null hypothesis: this is what pure search plus pure human knowledge achieves. Every RL result afterwards is measured against the fact that it needed no grandmasters. A footnote on the history: Kasparov was rattled by playing a machine and blundered uncharacteristically, and computer chess arguably needed another few years to be genuinely stronger. The 1997 date marks the perception, not quite the crossing. Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=19 Chinook's retrograde analysis is a second search running the other way: start from won positions, work backwards, and tabulate every position from which a win is forced. With 11 or fewer pieces on the board, Chinook stopped searching and simply looked up the answer. The Tinsley story is worth knowing. Marion Tinsley lost seven games in his entire career; two were to Chinook, in a championship match he had to abandon for health reasons before dying. Unable to settle it against the best human, Jonathan Schaeffer settled it against the best possible play instead — solving checkers outright in 2007, roughly 10^{24} positions. The reason two search-only systems open a reinforcement learning lecture It is a corrective, stated outright: it is easy to slip into believing you learn a value function or a network and then just apply it. In these domains search is the primary driver of performance, and you must evaluate the position in front of you dynamically. The rest of the lecture is about combining the two, not replacing one with the other. 4 · Self-play reinforcement learning p.20–21 · Self-Play TD and Afterstates ⏱ 42:38 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=20 \Delta\mathbf{w}=\alpha\big(v(S_{t+1},\mathbf{w})-v(S_t,\mathbf{w})\big)\nabla_\mathbf{w}v(S_t,\mathbf{w}) Almost nothing changes. Code still needs this terminal boundary condition even though the displayed interior update has no reward term. Two things do change, and neither is on the slide: You are estimating minimax values, not v_\pi for a fixed policy. Policy improvement improves both players at once — maximizing for white and minimizing for black — which is what drives the pair toward equilibrium rather than toward one player exploiting the other. In a deterministic game you have the model — it is the rules — so \text{succ}(s,a) is free, and q_ reduces to v_ evaluated at the resulting position. The saving is real: instead of a table over \mathcal{S} \times \mathcal{A} you keep one over positions, and many action sequences that transpose to the same position share an entry automatically. The precondition is deterministic transitions plus known rules. It fails the moment either does. p.22–23 · Logistello ⏱ 47:10 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=22 Deep Blue's features were written by grandmasters. That produced 1.5 million binary features. The only prior knowledge injected is which regions of the board to build patterns over. Everything else is learned. Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=23 Generalized policy iteration, batched: play a few thousand self-play games, regress positions onto outcomes (Monte-Carlo evaluation), improve greedily, repeat. Result: 6–0 against the world champion, and the first superhuman program in any classic game. The slide leaves out the ingredient that made it work Logistello ran a full minimax search using the learned value function every time it played a move. The policy improvement step is therefore not a one-step max — it is a deep search whose leaves are the current value function. The lecture calls this crucial. Reading p.23 as "MC evaluation plus greedy improvement" and stopping there misses why the method reached superhuman play at all. 5 · TD-Gammon p.24–26 · Non-Linear Value Function Approximation ⏱ 52:27 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=24 The board flattens into a binary vector with a small block of count features per location — is there one white checker here, two, three… — and that feeds a neural network with a single hidden layer of roughly 40–80 units. The only non-linear value function in the lecture's final comparison table. Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=25 Random initial weights, pure self-play, TD( \lambda ), greedy policy improvement with no explicit exploration — and it consistently converged in the reported experiments. The slide notes that the same recipe did not work reliably for other games and leaves both observations unexplained. Both anomalies have the same one-word answer: dice Why explicit action exploration was less necessary. Dice inject substantial state diversity even under a greedy policy. That helps coverage, but it does not mathematically guarantee that every useful action is tried. Why the neural network may have been stable. Silver's explanation is that chance outcomes smooth the effective value landscape: a single tactical line is averaged over many possible dice rolls. Deterministic games have sharper tactical discontinuities and the same recipe often failed there. Treat this as the lecture's domain explanation, not a convergence theorem. The algorithm still combines bootstrapping, non-linear approximation, and a changing self-play distribution — a setting that can diverge. Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=26 The escalation on this slide is the argument for search in miniature: Configuration Level zero expert knowledge strong intermediate + handcrafted features advanced (1991) + 2-ply search strong master (1993) + 3-ply search superhuman (1998) Even with the strongest value function of its era, search was still required to cross into superhuman play. Two extra ply were worth more than every handcrafted feature. p.27 · New TD-Gammon Results ⏱ 59:18 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=27 Tesauro returned around 2008 and simply trained longer on better hardware, with zero expert knowledge — raw features only. The expert features were a compute limitation, not a knowledge requirement Trained long enough, the zero-knowledge version massively outperformed the version with handcrafted features. More hidden units are monotonically better across the whole range, and the 10-unit network actually plateaus and decays while 80 keeps climbing. This is a 2008 result predicting the entire subsequent decade: the hand-engineering was compensating for a shortage of computation, and it stopped being necessary once the computation arrived. Could the features the network learned be read out and taught to humans? Not directly — but humans learned from it anyway, by watching it play. Interpreting the hidden layer is hard and largely was not done. What happened instead is that TD-Gammon changed how humans play backgammon. Players saw openings and strategies they had not considered, adopted them, and the human standard of play rose. The knowledge transferred through behavior rather than through weights. 6 · Learning from search values p.28–29 · Simple TD, and Where It Fails ⏱ 1:02:24 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=28 v(S_t,\mathbf{w})\leftarrow v(S_{t+1},\mathbf{w}),\qquad v_+(S_t,\mathbf{w})=\underset{s\in\text{leaves}(S_t)}{\text{minimax}}\;v(s,\mathbf{w}) Logistello and TD-Gammon both used a two-stage pipeline: learn a value function by TD, then later use it in a search. The search never improves the value function — it only consumes it at play time. Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=29 And the two-stage approach fails badly in chess and checkers. Why tactical games break simple TD, and what that implies A feature vector of piece counts contains no signal about checkmates, pins, or forks. Those are properties of the tree, not of the position's surface features. So a value function trained only on positions is being asked to predict something its inputs cannot see. The fix is to get search into the learning loop, not just the playing loop — learn directly from minimax search values, so the tactical information the search discovers becomes part of what the value function is trained on. The three algorithms that follow are three escalating answers to exactly this. p.30–31 · TD Root ⏱ 1:05:26 Silver - Lecture 10 Classic Games.pdf › page=30 v(S_t,\mathbf{w})\leftarrow v_+(S_{t+1},\mathbf{w})=v(l_+(S_{t+1}),\mathbf{w}) Update the value function toward the search value at the next state instead of its raw value. In words: I thought black was winning; I moved, ran a deep search, and found white is winning — so I should have known that without searching. The mechanical detail worth holding: after a tie-breaking choice, a deterministic minimax search has one selected leaf on the principal variation whose value propagates all the way to the root, so the search value is that leaf's value locally. Each slide is embedded below with only what the slide itself does not say — the reasoning, the caveats, and the questions worth being able to answer. The one idea L2 builds the MDP by adding one ingredient at a time, and each addition creates exactly one new question: Object Tuple New ingredient New question Markov process \langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{P}\rangle — what happens? Markov reward process \langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma\rangle reward how good is it? Markov decision process \langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma\rangle actions what should I do? Each layer inherits everything below it, so once you can evaluate an MRP you can evaluate any MDP with a fixed policy — because fixing a policy collapses an MDP back into an MRP (p.27). Two Bellman equations, and knowing which is which organizes the whole course Both say value now = immediate reward + discounted value of where you land. They differ in one symbol: \underbrace{v_\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a s)\big(\dots\big)}_{\text{expectation: average over your policy}}\qquad\underbrace{v_(s)=\max_a\big(\dots\big)}_{\text{optimality: take the best action}} Expectation → evaluation (how good is this policy). Optimality → control (how good is the best policy). The consequence is immediate and decides everything downstream: the expectation equation is linear and can be solved by matrix inversion; the optimality equation contains a \max , is non-linear, and has no closed form. That single fact is why L3 exists. Solving an MDP means finding q_ Not v_ . Knowing v_(s) tells you how much reward is available but not how to get it — you would still need a one-step lookahead through \mathcal{P} and \mathcal{R} to choose. Knowing q_(s,a) finishes the job: \pi_(s)=\arg\max_a q_(s,a) , no model required. Hold onto this, because L5 spends its first ten minutes rediscovering it as the reason model-free control uses Q rather than V . This is exactly the constant- \alpha argument in L4. (2) Absorb it into the state. If the probability depends on how long you have been somewhere, then how long you have been there is part of the state. Add a counter and the process is Markov again — at the cost of many more states, possibly infinitely many. Option 2 is the deeper point: "non-Markov" usually means "your state is missing something." Without it, a loop that keeps collecting reward gives \infty and the mathematics stops working. 3. It represents an imperfect model. This is the intuitive one: a plan promising a bigger reward in ten years requires you to trust your model for ten years. Discounting is how much you trust it. 4. The one idea L2 wrote down the Bellman equations and left them as equations. L3 does one thing to them: Turn the equality into an assignment, and iterate. \underbrace{v_\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a s)\Big(\mathcal{R}^a_s+\gamma\sum_{s'}\mathcal{P}^a_{ss'}v_\pi(s')\Big)}_{\text{L2: a fact about }v_\pi} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \underbrace{v_{k+1}(s)\leftarrow\sum_a\pi(a s)\Big(\mathcal{R}^a_s+\gamma\sum_{s'}\mathcal{P}^a_{ss'}v_k(s')\Big)}_{\text{L3: an algorithm}} Everything else follows from which Bellman equation you iterate. Slide p.26 is the entire lecture in one table: Problem Bellman equation Algorithm Prediction expectation iterative policy evaluation Control expectation + greedy improvement policy iteration Control optimality value iteration Why MDPs are a dynamic-programming problem at all DP needs two properties, and the MDP supplies each from a different object: Optimal substructure — the problem decomposes into subproblems. This is the Bellman equation: the value of a state is one step plus the value of the successor. Overlapping subproblems — the same subproblem recurs, so answers can be cached. This is the value function: a store of "how much reward can I get from here onward", computed once and reused everywhere it appears. That reframing is worth keeping: the value function is a cache. Every algorithm in this course is a scheme for filling it in. This lecture solves planning, not reinforcement learning Somebody hands you \mathcal{P} and \mathcal{R} — the full source code of the environment. Nothing here works without them, which is exactly the assumption L4 removes. Keep the two axes separate, because the course is organized by them: planning vs learning (do you know the model?) and prediction vs control (evaluate a given policy, or find the best one?). L3 is planning; both halves of the second axis appear here. Silver - Lecture 3 Planning by Dynamic Programming.pdf › page=33 One change fixes both problems at once, and it is the whole rest of the course Replace the full-width expectation with a sample: take \langle S,A,R,S'\rangle from actual interaction and back up that one transition. TD(0)의 target은 R_{t+1}+\gamma V(S_{t+1}) 이고, V(S_{t+1}) 는 아직 exact value가 아니라 현재 estimate다. 즉 한 guess를 다른 guess로 고친다. DP도 v_{k+1}=T^\pi v_k 처럼 이전 estimate v_k 를 쓰므로 bootstrap한다. 반면 MC target은 episode가 실제로 만든 return G_t=\sum_{k=0}^{T-t-1}\gamma^kR_{t+k+1} 이다. TD와 MC는 둘 다 sample을 쓰지만, TD만 bootstrap한다. DP는 bootstrap하지만 sample 대신 model의 full expectation을 쓴다. Q2. Non-stationary problem과 \alpha — 중간에 바꿔도 되나 슬라이드: Incremental Monte-Carlo Updates · Zotero p.11 · Random Walk: MC vs. TD · p.20 내 코멘트: “non-stationary problems?” · “ \alpha 가 크면 초반 error가 빨리 줄지만 나중엔 증가하는데, 중간에 바꾸면 안 되나?” Non-stationary는 같은 state의 return distribution 자체가 시간에 따라 변하는 문제다. 예를 들어 robot dynamics가 payload·마찰·battery 상태 때문에 바뀌면, 오래전 sample과 지금 sample을 같은 비중으로 평균내는 1/N(s) update가 변화 추적을 방해한다.
