Stationary problem에서 초반 속도와 최종 accuracy를 함께 원하면 decaying schedule \alpha_k 가 표준적이다. Tabular stochastic approximation의 대표 sufficient condition은 \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\alpha_k=\infty, \qquad \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\alpha_k^2 [!note] 식을 읽는 한 문장 첫 식은 “ (s,a) 다음에 어디로 갔나?”를 비율로 세고, 둘째 식은 “ (s,a) 에서 reward를 평균 얼마 받았나?”를 계산한다. MC가 mean-squared error를 minimize한다는 식은 왜 나왔나 이 식은 MC를 새 optimization algorithm으로 정의하려고 나온 것이 아니다. Finite dataset을 batch replay했을 때 MC update가 수렴하는 fixed point를 다른 방식으로 표현한 것이다. State s 에서 관찰한 return들을 g_1^{(s)},g_2^{(s)},\ldots,g_{N_s}^{(s)} 라 하자. Tabular MC는 이 sample들의 mean을 value estimate로 쓴다. Tabular는 뭐고 지금 알아야 하나? State마다 independent scalar를 하나씩 lookup table에 저장한다는 뜻이다. 이 예제라면 V[A], V[B] 두 칸이 전부다. Neural network처럼 여러 state가 parameter를 공유하는 function approximation의 반대말이다. 지금은 “각 state의 값을 별개 숫자로 저장한다”만 알고 넘어가면 충분하고, function approximation은 Lecture 6에서 배운다. V_{\mathrm{MC}}(s) =\frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}g_i^{(s)}. 그런데 squared-error objective J_s(v)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\left(g_i^{(s)}-v\right)^2 를 가장 작게 만드는 scalar v 도 정확히 같은 sample mean이다. Derivative를 0 으로 두면 \begin{aligned} \frac{dJ_s}{dv} &=-2\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\left(g_i^{(s)}-v\right)=0,\\ N_s v &=\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}g_i^{(s)},\\ v &=\frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}g_i^{(s)}. \end{aligned} Batch MC update 자체에서도 같은 관계가 바로 보인다. Dataset 전체를 한 번 replay해 s 에 대한 update를 합치면 \Delta V(s) =\alpha\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\left(g_i^{(s)}-V(s)\right) =-\frac{\alpha}{2}\frac{dJ_s}{dV(s)}. 즉 batch MC의 total update는 empirical squared error의 negative gradient 방향이다. 충분히 작은 step-size로 같은 finite dataset을 반복 replay해 update가 더 이상 움직이지 않는 fixed point에 도달하면 \Delta V(s)=0 \iff V(s)=\frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}g_i^{(s)} \iff V(s)=\arg\min_v J_s(v). Slide의 전체 식 \sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{t=0}^{T_k-1} \left(G_t^k-V(S_t^k)\right)^2 도 같은 objective를 모든 state의 visit에 대해 한꺼번에 쓴 것이다. Tabular setting에서는 V[A], V[B]처럼 각 V(s) 가 separate parameter라 state별 problem으로 분리된다. First-visit MC라면 episode마다 첫 visit의 return만 sample set에 넣고, every-visit MC라면 모든 visit을 넣는다는 차이만 있다. AB example에 직접 넣으면 더 단순하다. A 에서 관찰한 return은 단 하나, 0 이므로 J_A(v)=(0-v)^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad V_{\mathrm{MC}}(A)=0. B 에서 관찰한 return은 1 이 6개, 0 이 2개이므로 \begin{aligned} J_B(v) &=6(1-v)^2+2(0-v)^2,\\ \frac{dJ_B}{dv} &=16v-12=0,\\ V_{\mathrm{MC}}(B) &=\frac{12}{16}=\frac{6}{8}=0.75. \end{aligned} 여기서 중요한 한계: 이것은 finite dataset의 observed returns에 대한 empirical MSE minimizer다. Finite data에서는 true v_\pi 와 다를 수 있다. Data가 무한히 쌓이면 law of large numbers에 의해 sample mean이 v_\pi 로 간다. 그래서 p.24가 이 식을 넣은 목적은 finite data에서 MC와 TD가 서로 다른 답을 내는 이유를 대비하려는 것이다. MC: 각 state에서 직접 관찰한 return에 best fit → V(A)=0 TD: data로 \hat{\mathcal P},\hat{\mathcal R} 을 만들고 Markov structure를 공유 → V(A)=0.75 TD가 A 에서 보지 못한 reward 1 을 invent한 것이 아니다. “현재 B 에 도달하면, 과거 어떤 episode에서 왔는지는 future에 필요 없다”는 Markov property를 이용해 다른 episode에서 얻은 B 의 evidence를 A 에도 전달한 것이다. 그래서 Markov assumption이 맞으면 TD가 보통 sample-efficient하다. 반대로 observation이 true state가 아니어서 hidden history가 future를 바꾸는 non-Markov setting이면, MC의 complete return이 model misspecification에 덜 속을 수 있다. Q4. Unified View — sampling·bootstrapping과 수렴은 별개다 슬라이드: Bootstrapping and Sampling · Zotero p.29 · Unified View of Reinforcement Learning · p.30 내 코멘트: “다시 설명좀. 그럼 DP, TD는 참값에 도달할 수 없는 거임?” Unified View의 두 axis는 다음이다. vertical: sample backup ↔ full backup. 한 transition sample만 쓰는가, model로 가능한 successor 전체의 expectation을 계산하는가. horizontal: shallow ↔ deep backup. 몇 step 뒤에서 bootstrap하는가. TD(0)는 one-step, n -step TD는 중간, MC는 terminal까지 간다. 따라서 네 corner는 TD(sample+shallow), MC(sample+deep), DP(full+shallow), exhaustive search(full+deep)다. \lambda 는 shallow/deep 사이를 연속적으로 조절한다. Bootstrap한다고 exact value에 못 가는 것은 아니다. “Target이 현재는 biased”와 “algorithm의 limit가 biased”를 구분해야 한다. DP: finite discounted MDP에서 T^\pi 는 \gamma -contraction이므로 v_k\to v_\pi . 일반적으로 finite iteration에 exact equality를 찍지는 않고 asymptotically approach한다. Direct linear solve는 별도 방법이다. Tabular TD(0): fixed policy, Markov sampling, 모든 relevant state의 충분한 visit, 적절한 diminishing step-size 같은 조건에서 V_k\to v_\pi almost surely. MC: 같은 coverage와 sample-mean 조건에서 law of large numbers로 V_k\to v_\pi almost surely. 현실의 finite data·finite precision에서는 보통 tolerance 안에 들어오면 “수렴했다”고 한다. Constant \alpha 를 쓰면 TD와 MC 모두 stochastic noise 때문에 exact point에 정착하지 않고 그 근처를 계속 움직인다. Function approximation·off-policy learning을 붙이면 tabular convergence 결과를 그대로 적용할 수도 없다. Q5. n -step Random Walk graph는 어떻게 읽나 슬라이드: Large Random Walk Example · Zotero p.33 내 코멘트: “?” 각 curve의 label은 backup depth n , horizontal axis는 \alpha , vertical axis는 처음 10 episode 동안의 average RMS error다. 위는 online update, 아래는 offline update다. 여기서 bias는 무슨 뜻인가 Bias는 target이 항상 “높다”거나 “낮다”는 일상적 표현이 아니다. State S_t=s 에서 같은 experiment를 무한히 반복했을 때 target의 expectation이 true value v_\pi(s) 에서 얼마나 벗어나는가다. \operatorname{Bias}\!\left[G_t^{(n)}\mid S_t=s\right] := \mathbb E_\pi\!\left[G_t^{(n)}\mid S_t=s\right]-v_\pi(s). n -step target은 G_t^{(n)} =\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\gamma^kR_{t+k+1} +\gamma^nV(S_{t+n}) 이고, true value도 같은 지점에서 v_\pi(s) =\mathbb E_\pi\!\left[ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\gamma^kR_{t+k+1} +\gamma^n v_\pi(S_{t+n}) \;\middle \;S_t=s \right] 로 분해된다. 두 식을 빼면 reward 부분은 cancel되고 bootstrap estimate의 error만 남는다. \operatorname{Bias}\!\left[G_t^{(n)}\mid S_t=s\right] =\gamma^n \mathbb E_\pi\!\left[ V(S_{t+n})-v_\pi(S_{t+n}) \;\middle \;S_t=s \right]. 즉 bias의 출처는 아직 틀릴 수 있는 V(S_{t+n}) 로 bootstrap하는 것이다. 현재 V=v_\pi 라면 어떤 n 에서도 bias는 0 이다. n=1 이면 바로 다음 state의 estimate error를 target에 넣는다. n 이 커질수록 실제 reward를 더 보고 더 먼 state에서만 bootstrap한다. Episode 끝까지 가면 bootstrap term이 사라져 MC return G_t 가 되고, on-policy episodic setting에서 \mathbb E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t=s]=v_\pi(s) 라 bias는 0 이다. 0\le\gamma [!info] 여기서는 matrix norm이 아니라 value-error vector의 \infty$-norm State별 error를 하나의 vector로 보면 \lVert V-v_\pi\rVert_\infty =\max_{s\in\mathcal S}\left V(s)-v_\pi(s)\right , 즉 모든 state 중 가장 큰 absolute error다. 반면 matrix A 의 induced \infty -norm은 \lVert A\rVert_\infty=\max_i\sum_j a_{ij} , 즉 absolute row sum의 maximum이다. 기억법은 vector → max element, matrix → max row sum. 둘은 \lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\lVert A\rVert_\infty\lVert x\rVert_\infty 를 만족하도록 연결된다. → Matrix Norms › 4. Vector norm에서 induced matrix norm으로 단, 이 bound가 n 에 따라 줄어드는 것은 \gamma1 이면 해당 state의 update가 n step만큼 delayed되지만 episode 종료까지 기다릴 필요는 없다. Episode 뒤쪽의 target과 update는 앞에서 이미 바뀐 V 의 영향을 받을 수 있다. 같은 state를 다시 방문하면 이 차이가 직접 드러난다. Offline n -step TD Episode 시작 시점의 value estimate를 V^- 라고 하자. Episode 안에서는 V^- 를 바꾸지 않고 모든 update increment를 계산·accumulate한다. \Delta(s) =\sum_{t:S_t=s} \alpha\left(G_t^{(n)}(V^-)-V^-(s)\right). Episode가 끝난 뒤 한꺼번에 V(s)\leftarrow V^-(s)+\Delta(s) 를 적용한다. 같은 episode의 모든 target이 같은 V^- 를 기준으로 하므로 analysis가 단순하지만, episode가 끝날 때까지 새 information을 value에 반영하지 못한다. 현대의 offline RL과 다른 뜻 이 slide의 offline은 “logged dataset만으로 policy를 학습한다”는 현대의 offline RL이 아니다. 한 episode의 update를 끝에서 batch 적용하는 구현 방식만 뜻한다. 아주 짧은 n=2 timeline으로 보면: S_0\xrightarrow{R_1}S_1\xrightarrow{R_2}S_2\xrightarrow{R_3}\cdots Time 2 가 되어 S_2 까지 봐야 G_0^{(2)}=R_1+\gamma R_2+\gamma^2V(S_2) 가 완성된다. Online: time 2 에 곧바로 V(S_0) update Offline: 이 increment를 저장하고 episode 끝에서 V(S_0) update 이제 p.33 graph 다시 읽기 n=1 : bootstrap estimate를 일찍 쓰므로 target variance는 낮은 편이지만 current V error의 영향을 빨리 받는다. 큰 n : 실제 reward를 더 많이 보므로 terminal horizon에서는 bootstrap bias가 사라지지만 target variance는 커질 수 있다. 너무 큰 \alpha : online/offline 어느 쪽이든 update가 지나치게 커져 RMS error가 증가할 수 있다. Offline은 한 episode의 increment를 batch로 합치므로 stable한 \alpha scale이 online과 다르다. 두 panel의 같은 \alpha 를 완전히 동일한 effective update로 보면 안 된다. 이 experiment의 첫 10 episode에서는 online curve가 대체로 더 낮은 error를 보이지만, online이 모든 problem에서 항상 우월하다는 theorem은 아니다. 최적의 (n,\alpha) 는 problem과 update timing에 따라 달라진다. 따라서 서로 다른 n 중 하나를 고정하는 대신 전부 geometric mixture하자는 질문이 p.34의 \lambda -return으로 이어진다. Q6. 왜 \lambda -return에 geometric weights를 쓰나 슬라이드: \lambda -return · Zotero p.35 · TD( \lambda ) Weighting Function · p.36 내 코멘트: “왜 굳이 geometric weights를 사용하는 거지?” Continuing form은 G_t^\lambda=(1-\lambda)\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\lambda^{n-1}G_t^{(n)}, \qquad 0\le\lambda [!question] Backward view는 모든 s 를 update하는가, past states에만 뿌리는가? Forward view와 같이 실행하는가? Theorem의 s 는 무엇인가? → Forward and Backward Views of TD Lambda Forward view는 time t 에 서서 미래를 본다. 1. G_t^{(1)},G_t^{(2)},\ldots 를 만든다. 2. 이를 geometric mixture해 G_t^\lambda 를 만든다. 3. V(S_t) 를 그 target 쪽으로 update한다. 이 view는 “TD( \lambda )가 어느 target을 학습하는가?”를 설명하므로 theory에 좋다. Classical episodic forward view는 future reward가 필요하므로 episode가 끝나야 정확한 G_t^\lambda 를 계산할 수 있다. Backward view는 transition이 하나 나올 때마다 과거를 본다. 1. 현재 one-step TD error를 계산한다. \delta_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma V(S_{t+1})-V(S_t). 2. 과거 state들이 얼마나 “아직 credit 받을 자격이 있는지” eligibility trace E_t(s) 에 유지한다. 3. 같은 \delta_t 를 모든 state에 E_t(s) 만큼 나눠 보낸다. V(s)\leftarrow V(s)+\alpha\delta_tE_t(s). 그래서 backward view는 incomplete sequence에서도 step마다 실행 가능한 mechanism이다. 미래 return을 직접 저장·재계산하지 않아도, 나중에 생긴 TD error가 trace를 따라 과거로 전달된다. Q9. Eligibility trace의 식과 graph 슬라이드: Eligibility Traces · Zotero p.40 내 코멘트: “수식이랑 graph 설명좀” Accumulating trace는 E_{0}(s)=0, \qquad E_t(s)=\gamma\lambda E_{t-1}(s)+\mathbf 1\{S_t=s\}. S_t=s 이면 indicator가 1 이라 trace가 한 칸 올라간다. 그 state를 다시 방문하지 않으면 매 step \gamma\lambda 배로 decay한다. 자주 방문하면 decay하기 전에 1 이 계속 더해져 trace가 크게 쌓인다. 그래서 graph의 vertical jump는 visit, 내려가는 exponential curve는 recency decay다. Frequency heuristic과 recency heuristic이 동시에 들어 있다. Bell/light/shock 예제에서 shock 직전에 자주 울렸고 최근에도 울린 bell state는 큰 E_t 를 가진다. Shock가 만든 큰 negative \delta_t 가 오면 \Delta V(s)=\alpha\delta_tE_t(s) 이므로 그 state의 value가 더 크게 내려간다. Eligibility trace가 causality를 증명하는 것은 아니다. 최근·빈번한 predecessor에 credit을 배분하는 temporal heuristic이다. \lambda 의 역할도 여기서 보인다. \lambda=0 : 과거 trace가 즉시 사라져 current state만 update → TD(0). 큰 \lambda : credit이 더 오래 전 state까지 전달. $\gamma [!note] p.43–51의 theorem·credit matrix·offline/online 숫자 예제를 한 흐름으로 다시 보기 → Forward and Backward Views of TD Lambda 핵심은 TD error 여러 개를 더하면 중간 V 항이 cancel된다는 것이다. State S_k 가 한 번 방문됐고 episode 동안 V 를 고정한다고 하자. \lambda=1 이면 \sum_{t=k}^{T-1}\gamma^{t-k}\delta_t =G_k-V(S_k), 왜냐하면 \begin{aligned} &\delta_k+\gamma\delta_{k+1}+\gamma^2\delta_{k+2}+\cdots\\ &=\big(R_{k+1}+\gamma V(S_{k+1})-V(S_k)\big)\\ &\quad+\gamma\big(R_{k+2}+\gamma V(S_{k+2})-V(S_{k+1})\big)+\cdots \end{aligned} 에서 +\gamma V(S_{k+1}) 와 -\gamma V(S_{k+1}) , 그다음 항들도 전부 telescope하고, terminal value V(S_T)=0 만 남기 때문이다. 오른쪽 G_k-V(S_k) 는 정확히 MC error다. 일반 \lambda 에서도 G_k^\lambda-V(S_k) =\sum_{t=k}^{T-1}(\gamma\lambda)^{t-k}\delta_t 가 되어, forward-view \lambda -error와 backward-view trace가 같은 total credit을 만든다. 단, equivalence의 조건을 흘리면 안 된다. Classical theorem: episodic task에서 offline update, 즉 episode 안에서는 update들을 accumulate하고 끝에서 한꺼번에 적용하면 forward/backward TD( \lambda )의 total update가 정확히 같다. Classical backward TD( \lambda )가 step마다 V 를 즉시 바꾸는 online setting에서는 뒤의 target과 TD error도 바뀌므로 classical forward view와 일반적으로 exact equality가 아니다. \lambda=1 에서 offline TD(1)의 episode-total update는 every-visit MC와 같다. Online 중간 trajectory까지 MC와 같다는 뜻은 아니다. True Online TD( \lambda )는 수정된 trace와 correction을 써서 online에서도 대응 forward view와 exact equivalence를 만든다. 그래서 p.37의 “Forward view는 complete episode가 필요”와 p.39의 “Backward view는 incomplete sequence에서 online update 가능”는 모순이 아니다. 같은 최종 credit assignment를 이론적으로 정의하는 방식과, 그것을 실시간으로 구현하는 방식의 차이다. ⭐ 중요 표시해둔 것들 MC prediction: v_\pi(s)=\mathbb E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t=s] 의 expectation 대신 observed return의 empirical mean을 쓴다. First-visit와 every-visit 모두 tabular 조건에서 consistent하다. MC의 적용 범위: classical form은 complete episode가 필요하므로 episodic MDP 전용. “Model-free”와 “continuing task 가능”은 같은 말이 아니다. TD target의 variance 조건: exact target Y_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) 는 G_t 를 immediate transition에 condition한 expectation이므로 \operatorname{Var}(Y_t\mid S_t)\le\operatorname{Var}(G_t\mid S_t) . Learned V 를 넣은 target은 보통 더 낮은 variance를 노리지만, arbitrary approximation error가 있으면 이 inequality가 항상 보장되지는 않으며 finite-time bias도 생긴다. Bias–variance는 convergence와 동일하지 않음: Tabular TD(0)는 target이 finite-time에 biased여도 적절한 조건에서 v_\pi 로 수렴한다. n -step TD: TD(0)와 MC 사이의 discrete bridge. G_t^{(n)} 은 n 개의 실제 reward 뒤에 \gamma^nV(S_{t+n}) 로 bootstrap한다. \lambda -return: 모든 n -step return을 geometric mixture한 continuous bridge. \lambda 가 클수록 effective backup depth가 깊어진다. Forward view: target의 의미를 보여주는 theory. Classical episodic form은 complete episode가 필요. Backward view: one-step TD error + eligibility trace로 같은 credit을 과거에 online 전달하는 mechanism. Lecture 4의 결론: MC·TD·DP는 서로 완전히 다른 아이디어가 아니라, sample vs expectation과 backup depth 두 axis 위의 서로 다른 점이다. ✅ Annotation coverage Zotero item WNBKCHAI, attachment 2Y5BZHLB의 annotation 19개를 전부 대조했다. Asked: "bootstrap, on-policy, off policy 이런 용어 좀 쉽고 명확히 이해시켜줘" — 2026-08-19 chat, right after reading Silver RL Lecture 5 - Lecture Notes. Definition: bootstrapping means the update target is built using the algorithm's own current estimate, instead of waiting for the real outcome. V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\big(\text{target}_t - V(S_t)\big) The difference between methods is entirely in what target is: \begin{aligned} \text{MC (no bootstrap)} &: G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{T-t-1}\gamma^k R_{t+k+1} \\ \text{TD(0) (bootstrap)} &: R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1}) \end{aligned} G_t is the actual return the episode produced — no V estimate appears inside it, so nothing can be wrong except sampling noise. TD(0)'s target replaces everything after the first reward with V(S_{t+1}) , a guess that can itself be wrong. That is bootstrapping: fixing one guess using another guess, rather than waiting for ground truth. Analogy Checking a bank balance by taking yesterday's balance and adding today's transactions, instead of re-auditing the account from scratch. Fast, but if yesterday's number was already off, the error carries forward. Why it matters for L5 specifically: everything in model-free control bootstraps off Q instead of V . Sarsa's target R+\gamma Q(S',A') and Q-learning's target R+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(S',a') are both one-step bootstraps — same mechanism as TD(0), just on the state-action value. → L5 notes §5, §8 This restates L4 Q1 in the control setting — the concept doesn't change from prediction to control, only which function ( V vs Q ) gets bootstrapped. Full target-family comparison (MC / TD(0) / n -step / \lambda -return) is in Model-Free Prediction. Q2. On-policy vs. off-policy — what is actually different? Asked: same session, immediately following Q1. The one-line distinction: is the policy you're acting with the same as the policy you're learning about? Behaviour policy (acting) Target policy (learning about) On-policy \pi same \pi Off-policy \mu different \pi Sarsa is on-policy by construction, not by convention. The update Q(S,A) \leftarrow Q(S,A) + \alpha\big(R+\gamma Q(S',A') - Q(S,A)\big) is a sample of the Bellman expectation equation for q_\pi . That equation's right-hand side is an expectation over your own policy from S' onward — so the only way Q(S',A') is a valid sample of it is if A' is actually drawn from the same \pi you're evaluating. Break that and the target no longer estimates the thing it claims to. → L5 notes, p.22 question Q-learning is off-policy: it splits the action actually executed from the action used inside the bootstrap. Q(S_t,A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t,A_t) + \alpha\Big(R_{t+1}+\gamma \max_{a'}Q(S_{t+1},a') - Q(S_t,A_t)\Big) A_{t+1} (what you actually do next) is drawn from an exploratory \epsilon -greedy \mu ; the \max_{a'} inside the target implicitly samples the greedy \pi instead. You explore with one policy while learning the value of a different, better one. Why bother with off-policy at all (from L5 notes §7): 1. Learn from watching someone else act, and conclude you could have done better than they did — not mere imitation. 2. Reuse old data — GPI walks through \pi_1,\pi_2,\dots and discarding each policy's data is wasteful (this is why DQN-style methods are off-policy). 3. Explore however you like, while still converging to the deterministic optimal policy. 4. Ask several counterfactual questions off one single stream of experience. The non-obvious causal link: off-policy Monte-Carlo needs an importance-sampling correction multiplied across the whole episode, G_t^{\pi/\mu}=\frac{\pi(A_t S_t)}{\mu(A_t S_t)}\cdot\frac{\pi(A_{t+1} S_{t+1})}{\mu(A_{t+1} S_{t+1})}\cdots\frac{\pi(A_T S_T)}{\mu(A_T S_T)}\;G_t, and this ratio decays toward zero over a long episode — not just "high variance," but unusable. Q-learning goes one step further and needs no importance sampling at all, because sampling the Bellman optimality equation (which already contains the \max ) never required an expectation over \mu to begin with — it's sampling a different equation, not correcting a mismatched one. Bellman equation sampled Converges to Sarsa expectation equation for q_\pi q_\pi Q-learning optimality equation for q_ q_ So Sarsa-vs-Q-learning is not a style choice — it's a choice of which Bellman equation you're sampling, and on/off-policy status falls out of that choice mechanically. Q3. What is GLIE, and what does \epsilon_k=1/k actually mean? Asked: "GLIE에서 epsilon=1/k가 된다는게 뭔소린지 설명좀. GLIE가 뭔지 잘 이해 못했어 특히 두번째조건" — 2026-08-25 chat session. GLIE = Greedy in the Limit with Infinite Exploration. It's the requirement a behaviour schedule (how exploratory episode k 's policy is) must satisfy for MC control / Sarsa to converge to the true optimum q_ , not merely to some self-consistent value. \text{1) } \lim_{k\to\infty}N_k(s,a)=\infty \qquad\qquad \text{2) } \lim_{k\to\infty}\pi_k(a\mid s)=\mathbf{1}\big(a=\arg\max_{a'}Q_k(s,a')\big) Why condition 2 exists — the part that doesn't just fall out of intuition. The target we actually want to solve is the Bellman optimality equation, which has a \max inside it: q_(s,a)=\mathbb{E}\big[R+\gamma\max_{a'}q_(s',a')\big] If the behaviour policy stays soft forever — e.g. a fixed \epsilon=0.1 -greedy policy that never anneals — then the one-step target R+\gamma Q(S',A') , with A' drawn from that same soft policy, is not sampling the equation above. It is sampling the Bellman expectation equation for that specific soft \pi : q_\pi(s,a)=\mathbb{E}\Big[R+\gamma\sum_{a'}\pi(a'\mid s')q_\pi(s',a')\Big] q_\pi (weighted average over actions) and q_ (max over actions) are different numbers — a policy that keeps a permanent chance of acting randomly is worth strictly less than the true optimum. Without condition 2, the algorithm converges perfectly — just to the wrong target. The behaviour has to actually become greedy for the sampled equation to turn into the optimality equation instead of a fixed soft policy's expectation equation. Why \epsilon_k=1/k satisfies both. Condition 2 is immediate: \epsilon_k\to0 \Rightarrow greedy-action probability \to1 . Condition 1 is the subtler one — it isn't about whether \epsilon_k shrinks, it's about whether the sum of exploration probability across all episodes still diverges: \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\epsilon_k=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac1k=\infty \qquad(\text{harmonic series}) Even though each episode's exploration chance shrinks, the cumulative exploration budget over infinite episodes is still infinite, which is what guarantees every (s,a) pair keeps getting hit forever rather than being abandoned. Schedule \sum_k \epsilon_k Cond. 1 (infinite exploration) Cond. 2 (eventually greedy) Converges to constant \epsilon=0.1 \infty ✓ ✗ (never reaches 0) q_\pi of the soft policy, not q_ \epsilon_k=1/k^2 \pi^2/6<\infty ✗ ✓ some (s,a) can stop being explored early and stay wrong \epsilon_k=1/k \infty ✓ ✓ GLIE satisfied 1/k sits exactly on the boundary: it decays to zero (condition 2), but not so fast that the sum converges (condition 1). This is the same shape as the Robbins-Monro step-size condition ( \sum\alpha=\infty,\ \sum\alpha^2<\infty ) seen in Sarsa's convergence conditions and in L4 Q2 — "travel far enough everywhere, but eventually settle." The lecture notes' own caveat — "It is a valid schedule, not a good one"* — means other schedules satisfying the same two properties (e.g. 1/\sqrt{k} ) also work in theory; 1/k is just the simplest textbook example, not a claim that it's practically efficient. The ordinary semi-gradient update is not generally the gradient of one fixed scalar prediction objective, so the usual argument that every expected step descends a loss is unavailable. Special cases can admit alternative interpretations, but the generic update field need not be conservative. This is the direct consequence of the semi-gradient at p.18: ignoring the target derivative preserves a practical fixed-point update but gives up the ordinary regression guarantee. Gradient TD repairs the basic problem by constructing an explicit objective — typically the mean-squared projected Bellman error — and following its gradient with an auxiliary correction estimate. The slide marks Gradient TD as convergent across its table, including the non-linear column. Read that as the lecture's high-level map: exact guarantees depend on the particular Gradient-TD algorithm, assumptions, and function class. The \epsilon -greedy improvement theorem of L5 assumed you held q_\pi exactly; with an approximation, acting greedily with respect to \hat q_\mathbf{w} can produce a genuinely worse policy. Repeated evaluation and improvement can therefore chatter among policies instead of settling. Theory versus practice, stated plainly in the lecture Where divergence actually bites is neural networks. Apply naive Q-learning or Sarsa to one and it very often diverges: steep regions produce large gradients, a large step swings the policy, the policy change reshapes the value function, and the process spirals. With linear approximation, even off-policy where the table says ✗, it mostly works in practice — you have to try fairly hard to break it. The ✗ marks possibility, not frequency. Sample efficiency — each transition is reused many times, so you extract more from data you have already paid for. If they were the same, every update would move the target as well as the prediction, and with a non-linear approximator that feedback loop is what spirals out of control. Freezing w^- makes the target locally more stationary with respect to the network parameters. The replay buffer and its sampling distribution may still change, so this is not a fully stationary supervised-learning problem. Every few thousand steps, w^-\leftarrow w and the next phase begins. (s,a) → \hat q(s,a,\mathbf{w}) — action-in. state와 action을 둘 다 넣고 스칼라 하나를 받는다 3. s → \hat q(s,a_1,\mathbf{w}),\dots,\hat q(s,a_m,\mathbf{w}) — action-out. state만 넣고 모든 action의 값을 한 번에 받는다 2번과 3번은 같은 정보를 담는다. 다만 비용이 다르고, 그 차이가 뒤에서 중요해진다. 입력 출력 \arg\max_a 비용 Action-in (s,a) 스칼라 하나 action 개수만큼 forward pass Action-out s 길이 m 의 vector forward pass 한 번 control은 greedy action을 골라야 하므로 매 step마다 \arg\max_a \hat q 가 필요하다. 그래서 action-out이 훨씬 저렴하고, DQN이 이 방식을 쓴다 — Atari 조이스틱 18개 값을 forward pass 한 번으로 출력한다 (본 노트 p.39). Action-out에는 숨은 전제가 있다 출력층 유닛이 action 하나당 하나이므로, action set이 유한하고 고정되고 이산적(finite, fixed, discrete)이어야 한다. Action-in은 그 제약이 없어서 continuous action space로도 확장된다 — 대신 \max_a 가 lookup이 아니라 그 자체로 optimization problem이 된다. 이 한계는 Mountain Car에서 다시 나오고 (본 노트 p.25), L7이 policy-based method로 넘어가는 이유 중 하나다. 로봇 제어는 토크가 continuous하므로 직접 해당되는 문제다. p.8–9 — Which Function Approximator? Silver - Lecture 6 Value Function Approximation.pdf › page=9 후보 나열: linear combinations of features, neural network, decision tree, nearest neighbour, Fourier/wavelet bases, … 그리고 조건 두 개를 건다. 이 둘은 성격이 완전히 다르다. 조건 1 — differentiable. 미분 가능해야 gradient를 쓸 수 있고, gradient를 써야 값싼 incremental update가 가능하다. 이것은 편의를 위한 조건에 가깝다. 좋은 도구를 쓰기 위한 전제일 뿐이다. 조건 2 — non-stationary, non-i.i.d. 데이터에 맞는 학습법일 것. 이게 RL 고유의 제약이고, 강의 후반부 전체의 논지다. 두 단어를 풀면: non-stationary = 목표가 움직인다. control에서: \pi 가 계속 좋아지니까 v_\pi 자체가 모양이 바뀐다. 어제 맞춘 답이 오늘은 틀린 답이다 prediction에서도 마찬가지다: TD target R+\gamma\hat v(S',\mathbf{w}) 는 지금 업데이트하고 있는 바로 그 \mathbf{w} 로 계산된다. target을 계산하는 파라미터와 지금 업데이트하는 파라미터가 같은 \mathbf{w} 라는 뜻이다 non-i.i.d. = 데이터가 궤적(trajectory)으로 온다. i.i.d. = independent and identically distributed. supervised learning이 전제하는 가정으로, 데이터를 통에서 무작위로 하나씩 꺼낸다는 뜻이다 RL은 그렇지 않다. 지금 프레임과 0.03초 뒤 프레임은 거의 같다. 현재 위치가 다음 위치를 강하게 결정한다 이 두 단어를 붙잡고 있을 것 DQN의 트릭 두 개가 여기에 1:1로 대응한다 (본 노트 p.38): experience replay → non-i.i.d.에 대응한다 (버퍼에서 무작위로 추출해 상관관계를 없앤다) fixed Q-targets → non-stationarity에 대응한다 (target용 파라미터 \mathbf{w}^- 를 수천 step 고정한다) DQN은 새로운 발상처럼 보이지만, 실제로는 p.9에서 이미 예고된 두 문제에 각각 대응한 것이다. 이 구조를 알고 보면 DQN 슬라이드가 훨씬 단순해진다. 슬라이드의 오류 하나 (본 노트도 지적한다): p.9의 불릿 리스트는 p.8을 그대로 옮긴 것이다. They are not equally important: 1. Effective in continuous or high-dimensional action spaces. The practical number one. With a trillion actions or a continuous torque vector, \arg\max_a Q(s,a) is an optimization problem you must solve at every time-step. Policy gradient never poses it — it incrementally learns where the max is instead of recomputing it. 2. Better-behaved policy updates. A gradient step can change the policy smoothly instead of replacing it with a fully greedy policy at once. It can still overshoot with a bad step size and can still settle at a local optimum; the claim is comparative, not absolute. 3. Can learn stochastic policies. Sometimes necessary, for two separate reasons — p.6 and p.9. And the disadvantages, restated so they are not just words: Local rather than global optimum — see the four failed runs on p.22. Inefficient, high variance — you evaluate a policy by running it and watching what happens, which is noisy. The whole back half of the lecture is variance reduction. A student's answer that is worth keeping: when is a policy cheaper to represent than a value function? When the decision is simpler than the evaluation. In Breakout, computing that you will score exactly 1,714 points from here is a hard function to approximate. Encoding "if the ball is coming down over there, move left" may be trivial. The converse also happens — sometimes the value function is the compact object. Neither representation dominates; it depends on which of the two questions your domain makes easy. 2 · When you actually need randomness p.6 · Rock-Paper-Scissors ⏱ 14:39 Silver - Lecture 7 Policy Gradient.pdf › page=6 The uniform random policy is the Nash equilibrium, and any deterministic policy is exploited immediately. Here the environment contains an adaptive opponent — any regularity in your play becomes a pattern someone else optimizes against. Stochasticity is required by game theory, not by any deficiency in your state representation. p.7–9 · Aliased Gridworld ⏱ 15:25 Silver - Lecture 7 Policy Gradient.pdf › page=7 The features are (wall direction, action) pairs, e.g. \phi(s,a)=\mathbf{1}(	ext{wall to N},\,a=	ext{move E}) . Any function of those features — linear, neural network, your favorite thing — must therefore return the same output for both. It is not that the approximator is too weak. The two states are one state as far as the representation is concerned. Silver - Lecture 7 Policy Gradient.pdf › page=8 A deterministic policy must then take the same action in both grey squares. Move W in both, and from the right-hand side you oscillate in the corridor and never reach the money. Move E in both, and the same trap appears on the other side. This does not contradict the theorem from L2 L2 proved that every MDP has a deterministic optimal policy. That result holds under a Markov state representation — full observability, table lookup. Feature aliasing destroys the Markov property, so the problem is effectively a POMDP, and the theorem simply does not apply to it. Silver makes this dependency explicit. Keep the condition attached to the theorem, because the two statements look contradictory the moment you drop it. A single global \epsilon cannot express “mix 50/50 at this ambiguous observation, but act almost deterministically elsewhere” without unnecessary randomness in the rest of the state space. A parameterized stochastic policy can learn where to be random and how much. That is the capability this example is meant to isolate. The one idea Three lectures, three things to learn from experience: What you learn directly from experience Lecture a value function L4–L6 a policy L7 a model of the environment L8 Learning a model does not replace the learner. It multiplies the transitions available to it: most sample-based methods from L4 through L7 can consume a simulated tuple through the same update interface used for a real tuple. Whether the resulting update is valid still depends on model accuracy and on-policy/off-policy assumptions. The model turns finite experience into unlimited simulated transitions A real robot produces experience slowly and expensively. A model of that robot produces transitions as fast as you can compute. These are not new independent facts about the real world — every simulation inherits the model's errors — but they let the agent spend compute to propagate and test what its real experience has already taught it. This is the entire economic argument for model-based RL, and every algorithm in the lecture is a way of spending the second budget. Sample-based planning — the model's job is to produce samples, not probabilities Dynamic programming used \mathcal{P}^a_{ss'} to integrate over every outcome. Sample-based planning does not enumerate those probabilities; it asks a generative model for transitions. The probabilities are still present implicitly in the sampler. This often saves work because common outcomes are sampled often and very unlikely outcomes rarely. The consequence is that this lecture contains almost no new mathematics. Once experience is being generated, you reach for Monte-Carlo control, Sarsa, or Q-learning unchanged. L8's reply is simply: then learn \langle\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R}\rangle first. Every planning algorithm from L3 becomes available the moment you have a model. The argument that actually carries them is Silver's chess example, which appears on no slide: Why a model can be the compact object Chess has on the order of 10^{48} states and an extremely sharp value function — move one piece one square and a won position becomes a lost one. Learning v or \pi directly across that landscape is very hard. The model is just the rules of the game: move this pawn two squares and you are in that position. Trivial to represent, trivial to learn. So the sensible route to a good value estimate is to plan with the easy object rather than to learn the hard one. This is the general case for planning: there exist MDPs where it is very hard to say who is ahead without looking ahead. Isn't learning the reward function the same problem as learning the value function? No, and the gap between them is enormous. In chess the reward function is 0 at every non-terminal step and \pm 1 at the end. Learning it means learning to answer "is this checkmate?" — essentially a classification of whether the king has a legal move. Learning the value function means answering "from this complicated middlegame position, what is the probability White wins?" — which requires understanding the whole game. Reward is a local, immediate, one-step fact. Value is a global, long-horizon one. Model-based RL exploits exactly that asymmetry: learn the easy local facts, and recover the hard global ones by look-ahead. The disadvantage is real and worth stating precisely: you now have two sources of approximation error in series. The model is approximate, and the value function built from it is approximate, and those errors compound. Model-free RL has only the second. 2 · What a model is, and how to learn one p.12 · What is a Model? ⏱ 15:23 Silver - Lecture 8 Integrating Learning and Planning.pdf › page=12 \mathcal{M}_\eta=\langle\mathcal{P}_\eta,\mathcal{R}_\eta\rangle,\qquad S_{t+1}\sim\mathcal{P}_\eta(\cdot\mid S_t,A_t),\qquad R_{t+1}\sim\mathcal{R}_\eta(\cdot\mid S_t,A_t). "Model" is one of the most overloaded words in science; here it means precisely one thing — the agent's estimate of the MDP it is living in. Two simplifications are being made quietly: \mathcal{S} and \mathcal{A} are assumed known. Only \mathcal{P} and \mathcal{R} are learned. Learning the state space itself is possible and is a much harder problem. Transitions and rewards are assumed conditionally independent, so they can be learned separately. Convenient, not necessary. If you get to choose the features, why assume the state space is given? Because it keeps the lecture tractable — but the assumption is doing real work. The raw inputs you are handed may be useless for predicting dynamics even if they are fine for other purposes, and in that case the first thing you want is a better state representation. Silver concedes this outright: learning your own features is typically a very good idea, and learning the state or action space is a legitimate but more complicated version of the problem. Use the prose when an equation, condition, or figure needs explanation; leave Gaps to close for review. The one idea Every previous lecture reached for \epsilon -greedy and moved on. L9 finally asks whether that was any good. A fixed \epsilon gives linear regret, while a suitable decaying schedule can achieve logarithmic regret. The difficulty is choosing that schedule without already knowing the reward gaps. The whole lecture is one small matrix — a principle, applied in a setting: Principle Bandit Contextual bandit MDP Naive / random exploration \epsilon -greedy, softmax — \epsilon -greedy Optimistic initialization optimistic \hat Q — optimistic \hat Q / optimistic model (RMax) Optimism in the face of uncertainty UCB1, Bayesian UCB LinUCB UCB on Q Probability matching Thompson sampling — Thompson sampling on MDPs Information state search Gittins, Bayes-adaptive — Bayes-adaptive MDP Every row is developed in the leftmost column and then transplanted rightward. The final slide says exactly this, so the bandit section is not a warm-up — it is the lecture. The measuring stick is regret, and it turns the whole subject into one question Instead of "how much reward did I get", ask "how much did I lose against an oracle who knew the best arm from the start". Total regret decomposes as L_t=\sum_a\mathbb{E}[N_t(a)]\,\Delta_a — counts times gaps. That reframing makes the goal concrete: pull high-gap arms few times. And it exposes the central obstacle in one line, which the slide states almost in passing: you do not know the gaps. Every algorithm in this lecture is a different way of acting well without them. The classification that organizes everything — linear vs sublinear regret If you explore forever at a fixed rate, you pay a constant regret every step → linear. If you never explore, you can lock onto a wrong arm forever → also linear. Both extremes fail the same way and for opposite reasons. Sublinear regret requires an algorithm whose rate of mistakes falls over time. That rules out pure greedy in the worst case, fixed- \epsilon exploration, and one-shot optimistic initialization as general guarantees. Decaying \epsilon -greedy, UCB, and Thompson sampling are different ways to make exploration adapt with evidence. There is a whole axis of exploration that appears on no slide The lecture spends three minutes (⏱ 8:22) on a distinction it calls fundamental and under-discussed, and then never puts it on a slide: where you explore. State-action space exploration — \epsilon -greedy and everything else in this lecture. You track what you have tried where, and use that to explore systematically. Parameter space exploration — perturb the policy parameters and run the resulting policy for a while. This is what you do to an AIBO gait — L7 p.14. Parameter exploration buys consistency: you commit to a coherent alternative behavior and see how it does, instead of re-randomizing every step and executing a random walk. That matters in robotics, where per-step noise gets you nowhere. What it gives up is everything: it has no notion of state or action coverage, cannot recognize a state it has visited, and is really global optimization in parameter space presented as exploration. Nothing else in this lecture applies to it. Once regret is counts × gaps, "explore well" becomes the concrete instruction keep counts small where gaps are large. Two things the slide does not say: Why regret rather than raw reward. Regret compares an algorithm with an oracle on the same problem, separating learning loss from the problem's baseline reward. It is not invariant to reward scaling: multiply all rewards by c and regret also scales by c . *The gaps are defined against V^ , which is exactly what you are trying to find.* The decomposition is a diagnostic, not an algorithm. The curve has constant slope. Never explore and you can lock onto a suboptimal arm permanently, incurring that arm's gap every step, forever. Same shape, different cause. So the target is not "explore less" or "explore more" — it is an algorithm that makes fewer mistakes as it accumulates experience. Read the flattening curve as a falling mistake rate, not as a diminishing amount of exploration. p.10–11 · Greedy and ε-Greedy ⏱ 23:35 Silver - Lecture 9 Exploration and Exploitation.pdf › page=10 Greedy locks on, and the failure is subtler than "it picks the wrong arm". You can try the best arm, be unlucky twice, conclude it is bad, and never revisit it.
